articles.title: Russian forces strike Ukrainian metallurgical, chemical industry sites — top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces launched a massive attack, striking metallurgical and chemical industry facilities, as well as military-industrial and fuel-energy sector facilities in the Kiev, Dnepropetrovsk, Poltava, Odessa regions, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Last night, the Russian Armed Forces delivered a massive strike using high-precision land-based, sea-based, and air-based weapons, as well as drones, hitting facilities in Ukraine’s metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as Ukrainian port infrastructure facilities in Kiev and the Dnepropetrovsk, Poltava, Odessa Regions, as well as naval vessels operating on behalf of the Ukrainian military," the statement said.
Russia uses Tsirkon missiles in nighttime strike on Ukraine
Russian forces used sea-launched hypersonic Tsirkon missiles during a massive nighttime strike against targets in Ukraine, the Defense Ministry reported on Max.
"The Tsirkon missiles launched from the sea brought a tsunami and a tornado upon the enemy," the ministry wrote, attaching a photo of the launch in which it compared the massive strike to the Ninth Wave, which, according to ancient maritime legends, is the most powerful and deadly in a sequence of waves during a storm.
Russian forces encircle major Ukrainian strongpoint in DPR’s Dobropolye
Russian servicemen have completed the encirclement of a major Ukrainian strongpoint in Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) and are moving towards Aleksandrovka, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of the Battlegroup Center’s decisive operations, [Russian troops] have completed the encirclement of a major Ukrainian strongpoint in Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic and are moving towards Aleksandrovka," it said.
Russian forces encircle Ukrainian troops in DPR’s Dobropolye - top brass
The Russian Armed Forces have encircled the Ukrainian National Guard’s 4th and 15th brigades, as well as the 425th Skala assault regiment, and are now eliminating them, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The Ukrainian National Guard’s 4th and 15th brigades, as well as the 425th assault regiment Skala, have been encircled. [Russian servicemen] are now eliminating them," the statement said.
Russian forces strike tobacco factory in Kremenchug used for ammunition production
During a massive strike, the Russian Armed Forces hit the JTI Ukraine tobacco factory in Kremenchug, where the production of small-arms ammunition had been set up, the Defense Ministry reported.
"In the Poltava region: [the Russian Armed Forces hit] the JTI Ukraine tobacco factory in Kremenchug, whose production facilities were used to manufacture small-arms ammunition for the needs of the Ukrainian armed forces," the ministry said.
Russian Armed Forces strike Nova Post logistics center in Odessa Region
During a massive strike, the Russian Armed Forces hit two Ukrainian logistics centers in Odessa, as well as a Nova Post logistics center in the Odessa Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"[Strikes hit] two logistics centers in Odessa and a Nova Post logistics center in the settlement of Ilyichevsk, which were used for the storage and distribution of military and dual-use cargo intended for the Ukrainian armed forces," the statement said.
Russia hits dry cargo vessel with Ukrainian military supplies bound for Odessa
The Russian Armed Forces struck a dry cargo vessel transporting supplies for the Ukrainian military to the port of Odessa, the Defense Ministry reported.
"A dry cargo vessel transporting military supplies to the port of Odessa was hit at sea. <…> [Russian servicemen also] struck port infrastructure facilities in the Reni port of the Odessa region that was used for unloading and storing military cargo and fuel and lubricants intended to supply the Ukrainian army," the statement said
Russian forces strike industrial sites, logistics centers in Dnepropetrovsk region
Last night, the Russian Armed Forces delivered strikes on plants in the Dnepropetrovsk Region that manufactured products for military purposes, including the Interpipe Steel plant and three logistics centers of Sirius Extrusion in Dnepropetrovsk, the Defense Ministry said in a morning report.
"As a result of the strike on the Dnepropetrovsk Region, <…> a steel plant in Krivoy Rog that produced steel for military purposes, the Interpipe Steel plant in Dnepropetrovsk, a supplier of rolled steel for the production of long-range UAV components <…>, and three logistic centers of Sirius Extrusion in Dnepropetrovsk for the storage and distribution of cargo for the Ukrainian army, were hit," the report reads.
Russian forces hit JV CJSC Sofrakhim in Pavlograd that produced missile
The Russian Armed Forces hit the JV CJSC Sofrakhim in Pavlograd in the Dnepropetrovsk Region overnight. The enterprise produced fuel for the Fire Point’s FP-9 missiles and gunpowder, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of the strike, the following targets were hit: <…> in the Dnepropetrovsk Region: <…> a plant for the production of solid rocket fuel and gunpowder (JV CJSC Sofrakhim) in Pavlograd, which produced warheads and fuel components for Fire Point’s FP-9 ballistic missiles," the statement said.
Russian forces strike 3 Ukrainian radar stations in Dnepropetrovsk, Odessa Regions
Russian forces used Geran drones to strike three Ukrainian radar stations and a radio relay station in the Dnepropetrovsk and Odessa Regions, the Defense Ministry reported, releasing corresponding footage.
"Footage of the Geran-4 Seeker UAV strikes on three Ukrainian radar stations and a radio relay communications station in the Dnepropetrovsk and Odessa Regions. All the targets were hit," the ministry stated.
Russian forces strike diesel distribution center used by Ukrainian troops in Kiev
Last night, Russian troops struck a Fire Point plant in Kiev and a POL depot that the Ukrainian army relied on for diesel fuel supplies, the Defense Ministry said in a morning report.
"As a result of the strike, a Fire Point plant that produced components and warheads for Flamingo FP-5 long-range cruise missiles, and a Grandterminal POL depot that the Ukrainian army used as a logistics hub to receive and distribute diesel were hit in Kiev," the report reads.
Kiev loses over 1,300 troops along engagement line in past day
The Ukrainian army lost up to 1,315 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by the Defense Ministry.
The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 215 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, up to 200 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and roughly 170 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.
During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost more than 420 troops in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, over 270 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and up to 40 troops in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.
All Ukrainian attempts to break out of Kharkov Region encirclement thwarted
Russian servicemen thwarted all Ukrainian attempts to break out of the encirclement in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"All attempts to break out of the encirclement [in the Kharkov Region] have been thwarted," the statement said.
Russian air defenses down 629 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over past day
Russian air defense forces shot down six guided aerial bombs and 629 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over the past day, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down six guided aerial bombs, a rocket of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system and 629 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian warplanes, 284 helicopters, 243,259 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 30,994 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,780 multiple rocket launchers, 36,538 field artillery guns and mortars and 72,552 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.
Russian forces strike Ukrainian UAV assembly sites over past day - top brass
Russian forces struck sites assembling and storing Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and enemy deployment areas over the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, the ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces struck logistics centers, workshops for the production of unmanned aerial vehicles and their storage sites, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 148 locations," the ministry said in a statement.
Ukraine loses up to 40 troops in Kharkov Region encirclement
Ukraine has lost up to 40 troops in the Kharkov Region encirclement, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Ukrainian losses [in the Kharkov Region] amounted to 40 personnel and an armored vehicle," it said.
Russian forces expanding external zone of control in Kharkov Region
Russian forces are conducting active operations to expand the external zone of control near four localities in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry said in a report on Tuesday afternoon.
"Active combat operations are underway to expand the external zone of control near the localities of Posredneye, Novosyolovka, Petropavlovka, and Prikolotnoye in the Kharkov Region," the report reads.
Russian forces continue to tighten encirclement in Kharkov Region
Russia’s Battlegroup North continues to tighten the encirclement in the Kharkov Region and expand its zone of control, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The Battlegroup North continues to tighten the encirclement and expand the zone of control in the Kharkov Region," the statement said.
Russian forces inflict damage on Ukrainian army near seven communities in Kharkov Region
Units of Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted damage on the encircled Ukrainian forces in the Kharkov Region near seven communities, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The damage in the encircled area was inflicted on the enemy’s manpower and armor near the Krasny Yar, Potikhonovo, Buzovo, Reznikovo, Khripuny, Varvarovka and Grachovka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said in a statement.

articles.title: You still don’t have the cards: Did Zelensky bring bluff to Trump?
articles.body:
You still don’t have the cards: Did Zelensky bring bluff to Trump?
“You don’t have the cards.”
That was the message US President Donald Trump famously delivered to Vladimir Zelensky during their fiery Oval Office showdown in February 2025. Trump accused the Ukrainian leader of “gambling with World War III” and showing ingratitude for US aid, while pointing out that Kiev’s worsening battlefield position had left Ukraine with few cards to play in peace talks with Russia.
While the clash did not sever US-Ukraine ties completely, the deck has hardly been reshuffled in Kiev’s favor since. Thus the table was set for another Trump-Zelensky game in New York this week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Even getting a seat at that table was a late deal. Just two days earlier, Zelensky was absent from Trump’s publicly announced list of UN bilaterals, and Ukrainian officials said no meeting had yet been confirmed. In the end they met for 40 minutes.
The hand Zelensky holds is hardly stacked with aces. Instead, it contains an unexpected $27 billion defense shortfall, a desperate shortage of Patriot air-defense missiles, a fresh trail of corruption scandals, and mounting battlefield losses.
Opening bet: The refinery dispute
Trump had already shown his hand before the sit-down. Earlier this month, he blamed Zelensky for the diesel price spike gripping the US and Europe, which the US president said has been caused by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.
By the eve of the UN gathering, the US national average had climbed to a record $6.5 per gallon, a topic particularly sensitive for Trump ahead of the midterms.
According to the Financial Times, Trump pressed Zelensky during a weekend phone call to stop striking Russian oil refineries, with the paper’s sources claiming he wanted to ensure Russian supplies could reach the global market.
Trump went so far as to announce that Russia and Ukraine had effectively agreed to stop attacks on energy infrastructure. Neither Kiev nor Moscow confirmed the truce. Speaking to press in new York, Zelensky, who escalated strike intensity and targeting through his so-called 40-day plan, has now demanded that Russia take the first step, though he has continued to attack Russian fuel plants.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has called a prospective truce a “very good idea” and said Moscow was “always on the side of peaceful solutions.” He also argued that protecting refineries alone would not solve the global fuel crunch. The bigger problem, he said, was getting Russian petroleum products onto world markets, which required safe passage for oil tankers – something he said Kiev was not willing to guarantee.
Ahead of the meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also rebuked Ukraine over targeting US-linked ships in the Black Sea, adding that while it did so “probably not deliberately,” “that’s something that needs to be addressed.”
Desperate for Patriot draw
Zelensky has repeatedly sounded the alarm over deliveries of US-made Patriot interceptors, one of the few weapons in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of tackling Russian ballistic missiles. In July, he said the country’s stocks were nearly exhausted and asked Trump for an emergency “winter package” of 300 interceptors, warning that Ukraine needed them “yesterday.” Ukrainian air defenses failed to intercept even a single Russian missile during some recent barrage.
However, multiple media reports have indicated that Washington’s Patriot stocks are also low due to the Iran war, with American Patriot inventories in Europe said to have fallen “beyond critical” levels. While Trump has denied the shortfall, the Pentagon has publicly acknowledged the strain.
Earlier this month, Trump also suggested that Ukraine could receive a license to produce Patriots in a “less sophisticated version,” though no details on the prospective agreement have emerged in the immediate aftermath of the New York meeting. Multiple experts have pointed to numerous obstacles to the program, warning that any production facilities would be prime targets.
Zelensky is almost out of chips
Late summer exposed a glaring weakness in Zelensky’s gamble: an unexpected $27 billion defense budget shortfall expected by the end of the year – a figure that ballooned almost fourfold over the past several months.
Kiev subsequently asked for more money from its European backers – met with a tepid response whereby Brussels even refused to acknowledge the $27 billion figure.
The shortfall arose as a result of Zelensky’s much-heralded 40-day pressure campaign against Russia that involved the very strikes on refineries Trump reportedly asked him to stop. The escalatory attacks also triggered Russian retaliation against Ukrainian military-related logistics, including effectively closing the port of Odessa, which serves as a key hub for agricultural exports.
Ukraine’s $27 billion request “surprised and unsettled” European officials, according to the New York Times, with some of Ukraine’s backers reportedly asking questions about how Kiev is spending the cash and if it actually needs as much as it says it does.
The Trump wildcard
Kiev does have one fresh trump card to hope for – except it lies largely up the US president’s sleeve.
On Friday, Trump signed a new sanctions legislation first proposed by late Republican Senator and Russia hawk Lindsey Graham last year. The measure gives the US president authority to target Russian officials, banks, and the energy sector, and to impose tariffs of up to 100% on leading importers of Russian oil and gas. Zelensky specifically thanked Trump for signing it when the pair arranged their New York meeting.
However, Trump retains authority over sanctions waivers and the scope of restrictions and tariffs, while the bill does not mention China and India, the key importers of Russian energy.
In addition, the Trump administration has a recent history of easing sanctions on Russian oil. During the Iran war, the administration issued temporary exemptions allowing the sale and delivery of Russian crude already at sea to alleviate pressure on energy markets.
A busted flush
Ukraine has faced consistent frontline territorial losses for months, yielding ground to Russian advances while struggling to replenish losses through a brutal and deeply unpopular forced mobilization campaign.
 
Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, a key Kiev backer, revealed that up to 27,000 Ukrainian troops are killed or wounded every month and that Ukraine could face a “catastrophic” winter. Zelensky claimed in July that 50,000 Ukrainian troops have been killed (in February he claimed 55,000) and 400,000 wounded throughout the entire 4.5-year conflict.
The Russian Defense Ministry, in turn, assessed in February that Ukraine had sustained 1.5 million casualties during the conflict, with more than 500,000 lost in 2025 alone.
Trump himself has repeatedly pointed to Ukraine’s dwindling manpower as a reason for Kiev to stop fighting. During the Oval Office showdown with Zelensky last year, he told him: “Your people are dying. You’re running low on soldiers,” before urging him to accept an immediate ceasefire so that “your men stop getting killed.”
The joker in the pack: Corruption in Kiev
Zelensky’s inner circle has reportedly embezzled millions, and possibly billions, from the war chest, all while asking for more. Trump has also called Zelensky a “dictator without elections” – referring to the Ukrainian leader’s refusal to hold a vote despite widespread unpopularity, and resentment from possible successors he has sidelined.
Zelensky’s inner circle is widely suspected of massive crime, and some have fled the country. The biggest case to date remains the $100 million Energoatom affair, where a network involving Zelensky’s former close associate, Timur Mindich, forced contractors at the state nuclear giant to pay kickbacks of up to 15%. Mindich is in Israel allegedly laundering bags of cash while a former energy minister has been served with corruption-related suspicions and arrested.
Zelensky’s prosecutor general fled the country following accusations he was gathering compromising material on Western-backed anti-corruption agents in Kiev. The head of cybercrime at the same office was exposed for “protecting” a network of scam-call centers, a Ukrainian innovation Zelensky rarely touts abroad but which targets innocent people in the EU with all the contempt one would expect from an enterprise solely focused on profiteering. Ukraine’s scam-call industry is reported to generate up to $1 billion each month.
Zelensky’s current chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, has been pulled into the controversy, with media reports linking him to a money laundering scandal though he has not been charged.
During his first presidency, Trump said Ukraine was known for “tremendous corruption.” Since returning to office, he has also repeatedly opposed open-ended US financial and military support for Kiev.
When will Zelensky’s bluff be called?
That left Zelensky – who insists he hopes Ukraine may still win – heading into another session with Trump carrying a list of critical problems rather than a set of winning cards. The Ukrainian leader is having a tougher time than ever bluffing his way through such widely-known issues as a $27 billion defense hole, thinning manpower, shrinking hopes of securing Patriot interceptors, repeated corruption scandals, and growing pressure to explain how much longer he intends to continue the conflict.
And across from him sat a president who has been reluctant to cut Kiev any slack while treating the weakness as proof that Kiev should sign a deal with Russia. In this vein, Trump has already warned Zelensky: “With us, you have the cards, but without us you don’t have any cards,” adding that if Washington walks away, Ukraine will have to “fight it out” on its own.

articles.title: From Shaheds to missiles: How Russia is reshaping Iran's arsenal
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
From Shaheds to supersonic missiles: How Russia is reshaping Iran's arsenal
Russia has reportedly been helping Iran to develop an advanced supersonic cruise missile capability, offering Tehran something potentially more consequential than another weapons delivery: the technical knowledge needed to develop the system at home.
According to a Financial Times investigation based on leaked Russian correspondence, travel records, and military patents, the covert programme, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and has continued during the current US-Israeli war with Iran.
The programme has brought senior specialists from Russian missile manufacturer NPO Mashinostroyenia into direct contact with Iran's defence establishment. Their work has focused on helping Tehran develop ramjet propulsion, which allows cruise missiles to sustain supersonic speeds while flying through the atmosphere.
Iran has already built and flight-tested a ramjet propulsion system, although there is currently no evidence that a Russian-assisted missile has entered operational service.
Russian engineers reportedly analysed Iranian flight-test data and advised their counterparts on technical problems involving fuel systems, combustion stability, air intakes and engine nozzles.
The distinction matters. Rather than selling Tehran a finished Russian missile, Moscow appears to be helping Iranian engineers overcome technological barriers that have constrained their own programme for years.
If successful, that assistance could eventually allow Iran to manufacture and further develop a new family of advanced cruise missiles independently.
Closing a gap in Iran's arsenal
Iran already possesses the Middle East's largest and most diverse missile arsenal, including ballistic missiles, land-attack cruise missiles, and increasingly sophisticated anti-ship weapons.
Yet sustained supersonic cruise flight has remained a significant technological challenge. Tehran has pursued the capability for years. Iranian officials announced plans for supersonic anti-ship missiles in 2016, while two Iranian diplomats were arrested in Ukraine in 2018 while allegedly attempting to obtain components and documentation relating to the Soviet-designed Kh-31A anti-ship missile.
The military value would be particularly significant at sea. “A supersonic anti-ship cruise missile can fill an important gap in Iran's naval arsenal,” Farzin Nadimi, Senior Fellow at the Washington Institute, told The New Arab.
Unlike ballistic missiles descending from higher trajectories, a ramjet-powered cruise missile could approach a vessel at low altitude while travelling at Mach 2 or Mach 3, reducing detection and interception time. Iran’s anti-ship ballistic missiles have so far failed to strike manoeuvring US carriers or destroyers during the current conflict, while, according to Nadimi, a sea-skimming supersonic weapon would leave Aegis-equipped vessels considerably less time to respond.
“That is the threat to the Gulf of Oman/Arabian Sea picket that now holds the blockade,” he said.
The threat could extend further offshore if an air-launched variant were eventually integrated with more modern combat aircraft. Iran has been seeking Russian fighters for years as part of an effort to modernise an air force still largely reliant on aircraft acquired before the 1979 revolution. Leaked Russian documents indicate that a contract covering military aircraft for Iran was signed as early as June 2021 and continued to be implemented after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The first tangible result was the delivery of Yak-130 advanced jet trainers to Iran in 2023. At least eight are reported to have reached the country, providing Tehran with a modern platform for advanced pilot training and a potential bridge towards operating more capable Russian fighters.
The Su-35 would represent the much more significant step. Reports in July suggested that Russia had completed the first 20 fighters destined for Iran, part of what leaked documents have indicated could eventually become a considerably larger fleet, although deliveries and their eventual operational status remain uncertain.
Nadimi argues that pairing a supersonic anti-ship missile with such an aircraft could move the launch point away from Iran’s Makran coast and increase the risks facing US naval forces operating deeper in the Arabian Sea.
For the moment, however, the missile capability itself appears to remain developmental. Hamidreza Azizi, Senior Iran Analyst at the International Crisis Group, pointed to Iran’s recent unsuccessful missile attacks against US naval forces as evidence that Russian assistance “has probably not yet reached an operational level”.
From Iranian drones to Russian know-how
C430L nevertheless reveals how much the military relationship between Moscow and Tehran has changed since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Iran initially emerged as the supplier. From 2022, Tehran provided Russia with Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 one-way attack drones and subsequently helped Moscow establish domestic production, alongside transfers of short-range ballistic missiles.
Russia then adapted Iranian technology to its own battlefield requirements. Russian-produced Geran variants received changes to navigation, communications and warheads, while Moscow developed increasingly sophisticated tactics involving large numbers of attack drones and decoys. That industrial ecosystem is still expanding.
Satellite imagery from early September reportedly shows at least ten new facilities under construction at the Alabuga production complex in Tatarstan. Some of those modifications subsequently appeared in Iranian drones, suggesting that experience accumulated over Ukraine was already flowing back to Tehran.
Some of those modifications subsequently appeared in Iranian drones, suggesting that experience accumulated over Ukraine was already flowing back to Tehran.
“What we are seeing is that military cooperation between Iran and Moscow has not been a one-way street,” Azizi told The New Arab. According to the analyst, Russia has provided Iran with upgrades developed for earlier Shahed variants and information derived from their operational use in Ukraine.
Russian military intelligence cooperation has also contributed to Iranian war efforts, particularly by improving the precision of strikes against US bases in the region.
The missile programme takes this exchange further. Russia is providing expertise accumulated through decades of developing high-speed missiles rather than simply returning Iranian technology in modified form. The specialists involved reportedly included senior Russian engineers working on sea-launched missiles, aerodynamics, ballistics and supersonic ramjet propulsion.
That could have consequences well beyond C430L itself. If Iran masters the propulsion technology, it could potentially incorporate it into later missile designs without requiring Moscow to continuously supply complete weapons. In that sense, the programme points to a broader shift from transactions involving individual weapons systems towards cooperation that can strengthen Iran's own capacity to design, adapt and manufacture them.
A partnership with limits
This does not mean that Russia and Iran have become formal military allies. Their 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty signed in January 2025 expanded defence cooperation but stopped short of providing mutual defence guarantees. Moscow has also continued to calibrate its support for Tehran against its relationships elsewhere in the Middle East.
Azizi also distinguishes the relationship from Russia’s partnership with North Korea, which has extended to direct manpower support for Moscow’s war. Iran-Russia cooperation, by comparison, remains concentrated on “technology and intelligence rather than direct assistance”.
The slow progress of the Su-35 programme also illustrates these limits. Tehran has sought the fighters for years and, while recent reporting suggests production is now advancing, their prolonged absence from Iranian service shows how slowly some of the most consequential elements of military cooperation have materialised.
“So this all suggests that there has been a qualitative upgrade in military cooperation between Iran and Russia,” Azizi said. “But it also shows that neither side wants to make it public or go beyond a certain threshold, at least for now.”
C430L fits precisely within that model: strategically valuable, difficult to observe, and capable of strengthening Iran without requiring Russian forces to intervene directly.
Beyond Moscow
Iran’s wartime cooperation is also expanding beyond Russia. The Financial Times investigation places C430L alongside other reported transfers, including Russian Verba man-portable air-defence systems and Iran’s acquisition of a high-resolution Chinese satellite used to monitor US military facilities.
Washington subsequently sanctioned the Chinese supplier Earth Eye, alleging that satellite imagery had supported Iranian strikes against US forces.
Taken together, these developments suggest Tehran is using different relationships to address specific weaknesses exposed during recent conflicts: Russian experience for missile technology and drone development, intelligence cooperation for targeting, and Chinese capabilities for surveillance and other technological requirements.
This does not amount to an emerging trilateral military alliance. Russia and China have different interests in the Middle East, different relationships with Iran and different thresholds for involvement in Tehran's confrontation with Washington. What they do show is Iran's growing ability to draw on separate partnerships for capabilities that its domestic defence sector cannot yet provide on its own.
For Tehran, however, formal alliances may be less important than access. The immediate significance of C430L lies in a missile that could eventually make US naval operations around Iran more dangerous. Its longer-term significance lies in the model behind it.
After years in which Iran supplied Russia with weapons for Ukraine, Moscow is increasingly returning battlefield experience, intelligence, and specialised technological expertise.
If that exchange continues, some of the most consequential Russian weapons transfers to Iran may arrive without a missile ever crossing the border.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine trade blows ahead of Zelenskyy meeting with Trump
articles.body:
Russian missile and drone strikes across Ukraine killed at least four people overnight, officials said Tuesday, while a Ukrainian long-range strike damaged another Russian oil refinery.
The ongoing exchange of daily aerial attacks, while positions on the battlefield's front line barely change, provided a backdrop to the visit by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the United States.
Zelenskyy was due to meet other world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump, at the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The Ukrainian leader is hoping to recruit their help to end Russia's more than 41/2-year-old full-scale invasion of his country.
Russian President Vladimir Putin isn't due to attend the annual event.
The war, which Western officials say has killed more than 500,000 Russian troops, has had global repercussions.
The repeated attacks on Russian refineries, following Moscow's strikes on Ukraine's power grid, have caused international shortages of diesel and price spikes, according to Trump. However, the global crunch also came after the Iran war led to curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Zelenskyy also wants help to ensure the flow of Ukrainian grain and other farm products to world markets through the Black Sea. Russian attacks on cargo vessels have severely disrupted Kyiv's exports, hurting its economy and threatening global supplies.
French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday that his country would provide Ukraine with more radars to help protect its power grid.
He said on social media that he discussed with Trump the possibility of a truce between Moscow and Kyiv on strikes on energy infrastructure and a "moratorium" on Black Sea attacks.
Zelenskyy began his New York visit by meeting with U.S. senators, thanking them for what he called strong bipartisan support for Ukraine and for recently passing a tougher Russian sanctions bill that Trump has signed into law.
Peace and security will be closer once the bill is fully implemented, he said.
Zelenskyy said on social media that he briefed senators on his proposals for de-escalation measures that he intends to discuss with Trump later Tuesday.
The Ukrainian leader also plans to again press Trump to send more U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems that Kyiv desperately needs to stop Russia's ballistic missiles.
Ukraine said that it struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, southeast of Moscow, in an overnight attack.
Several drones hit their targets, sparking a large fire at the facility, according to a statement from Ukrainian special forces.
The refinery, owned by Rosneft, is a key fuel supplier for central Russia, producing gasoline, diesel, fuel oil and other petroleum products, the statement said. Ukraine said that it struck the same refinery last June.
One person was killed and four others were wounded in the Samara attack, regional Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. He said that "the enemy targeted industrial facilities," but didn't specify which ones.
The Russian Defense Ministry Tuesday said that its forces downed 297 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula.
Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine included anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and more than 200 drones, Ukraine's air force said.
The strikes killed four people in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration.
The strikes across Ukrainian regions damaged homes, businesses and storage facilities, wounding at least five people, authorities said. Five people were wounded in the capital, Kyiv, according to officials.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday that its forces struck metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as port infrastructure facilities in four regions of Ukraine.
They included a Fire Point plant in Kyiv producing components for long-range cruise missiles and a tobacco factory in the central Poltava region used to make small arms ammunition, it said.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia imposes restrictions near Estonian border amid mobilization concerns
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia imposes restrictions near Estonian border amid mobilization concerns
Key developments on Sept. 22:
- Russia imposes restrictions near Estonian border amid mobilization concerns
- Russian jet-powered drones strike Kyiv, injuring 8
- Ukraine confirms strikes on 2 Russian oil refineries in Ufa, Samara
- SBU says it foiled FSB-linked plot to assassinate K-1 kickboxing federation president in Kyiv
- Trump says he'll use Graham bill's Russia sanctions 'if necessary'
- Ukraine strikes Russian drone storage and launch site in Oryol Oblast, damages 5 launchers
Russia has imposed temporary restrictions in two districts bordering Estonia, limiting nighttime movement, access to parts of the Narva River, hunting, and the carrying of firearms in the border zone, Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR reported on Sept. 21.
The restrictions, introduced by Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB, are in force from Sept. 16 to Sept. 26 in the Kingisepp and Slantsy districts of Leningrad Oblast.
The move comes as security concerns grow in the Baltic region. NATO officials have warned about Russian drone incursions, airspace violations, sabotage, and other hybrid threats, while countries in the region have been strengthening air defenses.
Russia says the measures are aimed at strengthening border security and preventing violations of border and migration rules.
The restrictions also come amid discussions about a possible new wave of mobilization in Russia after the Sept. 18-20 parliamentary elections. If announced, it could prompt more Russian men to try to leave the country through remaining land borders, including Estonia.
Estonian authorities said they were monitoring the situation and did not see an immediate threat to the country, but could not rule out the restrictions were linked to a new wave of mobilzation in Russia.
Elsewhere along Russia’s northwestern border, Finland has kept its entire land border with Russia closed since December 2023. On Sept. 3, the Finnish government proposed extending its Border Security Act until the end of 2028, citing the continuing risk of such operations.
In September, Russia also carried out drone strikes close to Poland’s and Moldova`s borders with Ukraine.
In August, Lithuania said it has intelligence suggesting Russia could use Ukrainian-made drones to carry out false flag-style attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region.

articles.title: ‘Incurable headache’ to enemies: North Korea tests new weapon system (PHOTOS)
articles.body:
‘Incurable headache’ to enemies: North Korea tests new weapon system (PHOTOS)
North Korea’s missile agency has tested a “new-type weapon,” according to Pyongyang’s state media. Seoul said two short-range ballistic missiles were fired on Sunday toward the Sea of Japan.
North Korean reports did not specify what was new about the unit, saying only that the test was “of great significance” to the nation’s military. State media released several photos showing the launch of a road-mobile missile tipped with what appeared to be a hypersonic glide vehicle.
Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un oversaw the test and said that his country’s possession of “ultra-modern defense technology” serves as a deterrent and would “give the enemy an incurable headache.”
Senior officials from South Korea, Japan and the US held phone consultations on Monday to discuss their response to the test, Seoul’s Foreign Ministry said.
Local media linked the launch to the multinational Pacific Vanguard maritime exercise held in August and September. Warships from Australia, Canada, Japan, South Korea and the US participated in the drills. Pyongyang views US-led military exercises in the region as a threat to its national security and has frequently responded with demonstrations of military force.
In recent years, Kim’s government has abandoned Korean unification as an overarching policy goal and formally designated South Korea as a separate hostile state. The shift has not been fully mirrored in Seoul, although the government of South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has made some adjustments to its messaging in that direction.
Lee’s Democratic Party of Korea generally favors reducing tensions with Pyongyang, in contrast with the conservative People Power Party. In an interview with The New York Times last week, Lee suggested that some relief from international sanctions on North Korea could encourage it to slow its weapons development.
“I believe there is significant value in a trade-off between sanctions – which are not particularly effective anyway – and a stop to the development of additional nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology,” he said.
“Aiming for denuclearization under the current circumstances,” Lee added, “guarantees that nothing will be accomplished.”
US President Donald Trump has recently taken a more conciliatory tone toward North Korea. In August, he suggested that an in-person meeting with Kim could be arranged after the Pentagon cut short a joint military exercise with Seoul.
The Trump administration’s international standing has suffered a number of blows recently, primarily due to his decision to launch a war with Iran, which has significantly disrupted the global energy market.

articles.title: Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed
articles.body:
A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, thought other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation.
The Center for a New American Security’s report, “Drones, Missiles, and the U.S. Munitions Shortage: The Role of Affordable Mass in a Taiwan Conflict,” released Sept. 18, makes the case for increased long-range weapons to strike Chinese military targets to thwart a takeover of Taiwan.
The report, authored by Philip Sheers and Stacie Pettyjohn, notes a gap between the number of targets the U.S. would need to strike and its diminishing stockpiles, given the ongoing use of such weapons in the conflict with Iran.
“In a U.S.-China conflict over Taiwan that is likely to become protracted, the inventory depth and disruption that lower-cost systems can provide will be invaluable to reversing U.S. disadvantages and stopping China from achieving its operational objectives,” Sheers and Pettyjohn write.
To close the gap, the report recommends both stockpiling high-end missiles and massing cheap drones and munitions to overwhelm a Chinese attack. Other recommendations include:
- Multiyear funding and contracts so manufacturers can expand weapons production capacity and the Pentagon can rebuild long-range missile stores
- Funding for cheap, long-range anti-ship and land-attack weapons to quickly fill inventory gaps.
- Standardized shared components across airframes to lower costs and scale production.
- Pairing inexpensive drones with advanced missiles to drain enemy air defenses.
- Prioritizing easily built designs rather than over-engineering
- Routing updates and briefings to Congress on these issues
The White House and Pentagon have taken steps to boost munitions production this year, especially low-cost weapons.
In July, the Pentagon announced multiyear framework agreements with Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies to mass-produce missiles for the Air Force, followed by a Sept. 17 announcement that Lockheed Martin would expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.
The former announcement is part of USAF’s Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program, unveiled in the fiscal 2026 budget with plans to ramp up such production to hit 5,300 missiles a year by 2028 and reach nearly 8,000 missiles a year by 2031.
The current projected five-year budget for FAMM is more than $12 billion for nearly 27,000 missiles.
Retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, now with AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the CNAS report’s call for more munitions is necessary. But he cautioned that the report’s focus on making weapons affordable needs to be tweaked.
“It should not be about buying cheaper weapons; it should be about how to optimize cost per effect in the battlespace,” Gunzinger said.
The Air Force must fight asymmetrically and maximize the effect of each strike, regardless of munition or platform, and there’s a middle ground for weapons and platform development and procurement, Gunzinger argued.
Precision-guided, specialized weapons such as the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile and the platforms that deliver them are pricey, and lower-end, short-range munitions for stationary targets have their place, but Gunzinger said defense planners can often make too much of a tradeoff if they focus too much on price to the detriment of capability.
“Now you’ve got something that, ‘OK, you hit a price point, but is it going to survive long enough to do its mission?’” Gunzinger said. “Is it going to be able to shoot its weapon before it dies?”
A Numbers Game
The CNAS report’s operational and tactical focus is countering a People’s Liberation Army attack on Taiwan with strikes against PLA ships—destroyers and amphibious assault ships—and hitting airfields on the periphery of the country, close to the Taiwan Strait.
But it does not include a plan to hit the Chinese mainland interior.
“The paper focuses on denying a PLA joint island landing campaign without considering strategic attacks to deny sanctuaries to the PLA and collapse China’s ability to maintain the offensive,” Gunzinger said. “This risks reducing a conflict with the PLA over Taiwan to a force-on-force math problem, like how many weapons and aircraft are needed to attack PLA forces located in the Taiwan Strait and coastal China. It risks becoming a numbers game.”
Because striking mainland China in a Taiwan invasion scenario might be required, Gunzinger said the current 500-nautical-mile limit of most affordable strike options undermines the CNAS report’s conclusion that more mass will equate to victory.
“China has the capability to project outer and inner rings of airborne and sea-based air defense sensors and shooters to defend its cross-Strait forces and operations,” Gunzinger said.
And using nonstealthy drones to approach the Chinese coastline to then launch affordable missiles doesn’t work either, he said. “This would likely result in losses of the aircraft and their weapons.”
“We win part of the battle,” Gunzinger said. “They win the war.”
Breaking a Stalemate
The numbers-on-numbers approach is what has led to a stalemate in the Russia-Ukraine War, said retired Navy Cmdr. J. Michael Dahm, now a senior fellow for aerospace and China studies at Mitchell.
“Just because you can generate mass doesn’t mean that you’re going to achieve your effects,” Dahm told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “You may be able to keep your adversary off balance, but if you’re not going to then judo throw him into what you want him to do, you’re just engaging in this kind of protracted, endless warfare.”
Throughout the history of the modern Chinese military, it has mostly been defense-oriented, Dahm said. The PLA has airfields dotting its landscape and hardened sites to pull and rotate forces from, as well as a layered air defense network.
What could overwhelm the Chinese defenses, however, is what the U.S. has seen poke through its defenses recently in the Middle East, Dahm said. Iranian air attacks have used a combination of low-end munitions and cheap drones with more expensive and capable missiles fired from various angles, locations, and at varying rates of speed to confuse and defeat air defenses.
This aligns with one of the report’s recommendations—for the Pentagon to develop new operational concepts that pair cheap and high-end weapons for mixed attacks.
“Using low-cost drones in the opening wave to identify air defenses, consume interceptors, and relay targeting data to follow-on missiles offers a promising and sustainable way to create repeated air base disruption,” according to the report. “High-end weapons should be preserved for more challenging targets, while affordable mass should be integrated into strike plans to service soft targets and to saturate air defenses.”
“The Iranians have figured out how to be effective: … send a whole bunch of slow-moving drones with a couple of cruise missiles and a couple of ballistic missiles,” Dahm said.
That’s because modern air defenders must set their systems to track certain ranges, altitudes, and speeds of whatever is in the airspace. And they can’t track everything effectively all at once.
“I don’t want a flock of birds showing up on my radar, so I set the speed gate for higher speed, but how high do I set it for? 100 knots or do I set it for Mach 3? What am I looking for? Range. How far am I looking? Altitude. Am I looking high? Am I looking low?” Dahm said.
Those factors mean an air defense system can’t stop everything.
“The way you overwhelm even the most sophisticated air defense system is you send some slow stuff, you send some medium stuff, and then you send these ballistic missiles that are screaming in from the upper atmosphere at Mach 3-4-5,” Dahm said. “It is hard for any modern air defense system to deal with all those inputs.”
While Iran is using that method against the U.S., Dahm advocates the U.S. use the same strategy in a Taiwan scenario against the PLA.
“That is absolutely what we should be doing,” Dahm said.
For example, to strike a Chinese military ship, such as a cruiser, Dahm said U.S. or coalition countries wouldn’t only send the same type of missile from one direction. They would simultaneously target the ship from air, land, sea, and subsurface platforms with a variety of projectiles at varying speeds and ranges, though the centerpiece of the assault might be an LRASM.
“You might send two LRASMs, but you need to accompany that with some of these more cost-effective missiles,” he said. “It is the reason we need the cost-effectiveness and the affordability, because we shouldn’t have an expectation that all of those weapons are going to work.”

articles.title: IN BRIEF: Military-industrial, energy, metallurgy facilities hit in strike by Russian army
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces carried out a massive strike on Ukraine’s metallurgical, chemical, military-industrial, and fuel and energy facilities in Kiev, and in the Dnepropetrovsk, Poltava, and Odesa Regions, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has summarized the main information on the results of the strikes.
Defense Ministry’s statement
- The Russian Armed Forces launched a massive strike using precision land-, sea-, and air-based weapons, as well as unmanned aerial vehicles, against targets in Ukraine overnight, the ministry reported.
- The strikes targeted facilities in the metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as Ukrainian port infrastructure in Kiev and the Dnepropetrovsk, Poltava, and Odessa Regions, and naval vessels operating on behalf of the Ukrainian armed forces, it stated.
- During the massive nighttime strike, Russian troops used sea-launched Tsirkon hypersonic missiles, the ministry reported on its Max channel.
Targets destroyed
- According to the ministry, an industrial facility in Kiev (Fire Point LLC), which manufactured components and warheads for FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, and a fuel and lubricants warehouse (Grandterminal LLC), used by the Ukrainian armed forces as a logistics hub for receiving and distributing diesel fuel, were struck in Kiev.
- Also, in Kremenchug, Poltava Region, the JTI Ukraine tobacco factory was struck. Its production facilities were being used to manufacture small-arms ammunition for the needs of the Ukrainian armed forces.
- In addition, Russian forces hit a steel mill in Krivoy Rog, Dnepropetrovsk Region, which produced steel products for military manufacturing.
- A pipe rolling mill (Interpipe Steel) in Dnepropetrovsk that manufactured and supplied rolled metal products for the production of components (fuselages, power units, wings, and other elements) for long-range UAVs was also struck.
- In addition, three Sirius Extrusion logistics centers in Dnepropetrovsk that stored and distributed cargo intended to supply the Ukrainian armed forces, were struck.
- A facility producing solid rocket propellant and gunpowder (Sovrakhim) was struck in Pavlograd, Dnepropetrovsk Region. It manufactured warheads and rocket propellant components for Fire Point’s FP-9 ballistic missiles.
- In addition, a railway infrastructure facility in Vinnitsa was struck.
- Russian forces hit two logistics centers in Odessa and a Nova Post logistics center in Ilyichevsk, Odessa Region, which were used to store and distribute military and dual-use cargo for the Ukrainian armed forces.
- Furthermore, a dry cargo ship delivering military cargo to the Odessa port was struck at sea.
- Port infrastructure facilities used for unloading and storing military cargo and fuel and lubricants intended to supply the Ukrainian army were struck at the Reni port in the Odessa Region.
Situation in Ukraine
- Ukrainian media reported explosions in Kiev, Dnepropetrovsk, Kropivnitsky, Krivoy Rog, and Chernigov overnight and on Tuesday morning.
- A fire broke out at warehouses in Kiev, the city’s military administration reported.
- According to information published on its Telegram channel, the warehouse facilities are located in the Goloseyevsky district of the city.
- A production facility, warehouses, and a factory were damaged as a result of explosions in the Kiev Region, said Timur Tkachenko, the head of the regional administration.
- According to information published on his Telegram channel, warehouses, production facilities, and an enterprise located in the Bucha, Obukhov, Brovary, and Belaya Tserkov districts of the Kiev Region, were hit.
- Industrial facilities in Dnepropetrovsk, Krivoy Rog, and Pavlograd in the Dnepropetrovsk Region in southeastern Ukraine were damaged and caught fire as a result of the strikes, the head of the regional administration, Alexander Ganza, reported.
- About 100,000 customers were left without electricity in the Chernigov Region in northern Ukraine as a power facility was damaged in the neighboring region, the Chernigovoblenergo regional power distribution company reported.
- According to the company’s Telegram channel, customers in four districts of the region--Koryukovsky, Novgorod-Seversky, Nezhinsky, and Chernigovsky--were left without power.
- The location of the damaged power facility was not specified.
- A critical infrastructure facility was damaged in the Poltava Region in northeastern Ukraine, according to the regional administration head Vitaly Dyakovnich.
- The facility is located in the Kremenchug district, he reported on Telegram.
- A local industrial enterprise was also damaged.
- Odessa in southern Ukraine is covered in black smoke due to a fire on the outskirts of the city. The authorities are conducting air quality measurements, Sergey Lysak, the head of the city’s military administration, said.
- Nova Post warehouses are burning on the outskirts of Odessa, the Ukrainian online publication Strana reported.

articles.title: Last September, Poland downed four of 19 Russian drones. This September, drone reached NATO’s missile shield in Redzikowo, and troops guarding it called 112
articles.body:
An unknown drone has flown right up to the US missile-defense base in northern Poland, and how the military responded has raised questions about how well the site is protected from the air. Rather than shoot the drone down near Redzikowo, a cornerstone of NATO's missile shield, the unit followed a set of procedures that included a call to 112, Poland's civilian emergency line, Onet reported.
Meanwhile, European intelligence officials are considering the possibility that Russia could test NATO’s resolve in the near future. According to one official, a potential attack could occur “within months, not years," The Guardian reports. 
Surveillance systems detected the drone about half a kilometer from the base on 15 September, where it operated for roughly five minutes.
This incident is linked to a similar one in 2025. Almost a year ago, also in September, around 19 Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace. Poland shot down only four Russian drones with modern Polish F-16s and Dutch F-35s. Meanwhile, Ukraine downs 87.4% of Russian long-range drones. Poland only shot down 17-21% of the drones that entered its airspace.
The base sits at the heart of NATO's shield
Redzikowo hosts the US Navy's Aegis Ashore installation, an American component of NATO's missile-defense system and one of the most sensitive military sites in Poland. It matters strategically to Poland, NATO, and the US. While American personnel guard it, Poland has taken primary responsibility for its security and assigned a dedicated unit.
Even before the base opened, there were efforts to secure anti-drone systems for it, on the logic that a site best protected from the ground can stay exposed from the air.
The ministry keeps its methods quiet
The Polish Defense Ministry says it established where the operator was flying from, notified the relevant services, including the police, and treats every case of unauthorized drone activity near a guarded site seriously. What it will not say is whether it tried to neutralize the drone, or whether the anti-drone and electronic-warfare systems at Redzikowo were used at all, citing security.
Warnings pile up across the flank
The stakes are rising along NATO's eastern edge. Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament on 17 September that, by the assessment of NATO, Ukrainian, and US intelligence, Russia's plans include drone and missile strikes on countries backing Ukraine, Poland among them, possibly staged to look "accidental" and test whether Article 5 means anything. Warsaw insists it is ready and will hit back at any attack. The Redzikowo drone, and the four-of-nineteen record behind it, are why that confidence keeps drawing questions.
