articles.title: Trump threatens Iran with ‘hell’ at UN, predicts deal after US midterm elections
articles.body:
President Donald Trump used his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday to defend an increasingly interventionist foreign policy, casting himself as a leader willing to use American military, diplomatic and economic power while declaring that the United States would continue to put its own interests first.
“While others have talked, I have acted,” Trump said. “While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them.”
Much of the speech focused on Iran and the nearly seven-month war that has reshaped the Middle East and disrupted global energy markets. Trump defended his decision to go to war alongside Israel earlier this year and said Tehran had rejected previous efforts to reach an agreement that would prevent it from obtaining nuclear weapons.
Trump said he now faced what he called a “big decision” over whether to reach a deal that would allow Iran to recover or move toward far more destructive military action.
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, before saying he nevertheless expected an agreement after the November midterm elections.
Trump said Iranian leaders were waiting to see how Republicans performed in the midterms, though he stressed that he himself was not on the ballot.
“The Republican Party is running, and I’m going to help them,” he said, adding that his principal concern remained ensuring that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon.
He also rejected reports that concerns over depleted US ammunition and interceptor stocks were constraining his military options, saying the United States possessed large quantities of weapons and was replenishing them rapidly.
Trump called on other countries to join Washington in economically isolating Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping, abandons its nuclear ambitions and stops supporting terrorism.
The war with Iran has complicated Trump’s effort to portray his foreign policy as a series of successful peace interventions. The Wall Street Journal reported that the White House is seeking to present his international record as a collection of tangible wins for Americans ahead of the midterms, even as the wars involving Iran and Ukraine continue to weigh on energy prices and global trade.
Trump invokes Oct. 7 and Gaza deal
Trump also invoked Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, accusing Iran of supporting the terrorists responsible and arguing that Tehran could never be permitted to operate under the protection of a nuclear arsenal.
He said Iran’s supreme leader had celebrated the massacre and described the threat posed by a nuclear-armed Islamic Republic as one the United States could not ignore.
Trump then pointed to Gaza as evidence of what he described as his ability to turn conflict into negotiated outcomes.
He recalled that when he addressed the General Assembly a year earlier, the Gaza war was still underway and hostages remained in Hamas captivity. His administration’s 20-point plan was later endorsed by the UN Security Council, and the Board of Peace was established to oversee the postwar framework. The board says the ceasefire brought the return of all hostages and is now focused on demilitarization, Palestinian civilian administration, reconstruction and humanitarian assistance.
Trump thanked Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and other countries contributing to Gaza, saying their money was reaching areas where humanitarian needs remain acute.
He also praised countries that have committed personnel, police or training to Gaza stabilization efforts, including Indonesia, Morocco, Albania, Kosovo, Kazakhstan, Egypt and Jordan.
The Board of Peace is scheduled to meet on the sidelines of the General Assembly to review implementation of the Gaza framework and discuss its next priorities.
Ukraine, Greenland and Venezuela next
Trump devoted less time to Russia’s war against Ukraine, saying his administration was continuing efforts to bring the conflict to an end.
His diplomatic agenda after the speech underscored how much unfinished business remains.
He was scheduled to meet separately with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Gulf leaders, with the Iran war expected to feature prominently in the regional discussions. The continuing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine have both contributed to pressure on global energy markets.
Trump was also expected to sign an agreement expanding the US military and commercial presence in Greenland after nearly two years of pressure on Denmark, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Another meeting was set with Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, whose government has entered into an arrangement giving the Pentagon a stake in the country’s oil sector. Trump has argued that closer US involvement in Venezuelan energy production will help lower fuel prices at home.
The meeting is politically sensitive because Rodríguez was a senior figure in the government of Nicolás Maduro, who was removed in a US military operation earlier this year. Trump has emphasized cooperation with Rodríguez while moving more slowly on a transition to democratic government, according to the Journal.
Xi summit looms
Trump’s UN appearance also comes on the eve of a three-day state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The two leaders are expected to discuss artificial intelligence, rare earth minerals and Taiwan, among other issues. The Journal reported that Trump, who previously took a more confrontational approach toward Beijing, is now seeking a less adversarial relationship and wants to avoid a deepening economic and military confrontation.
The summit is expected to focus heavily on optics and the broader relationship rather than major new agreements.
Trump’s packed schedule reflects the contrast at the heart of his UN message: he presented himself as a president who has already delivered peace through decisive action, even as some of the largest crises he has confronted remain unresolved.
His Iran policy captures that tension most clearly. Trump threatened Tehran with potentially devastating consequences while simultaneously predicting that diplomacy would ultimately prevail.
“The president is open to a meeting with him or anybody,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian ahead of the speech, while cautioning that Iran’s supreme leader remains the country’s ultimate decision-maker.
For Trump, the message to the General Assembly was that willingness to negotiate and willingness to use force are not contradictory elements of his foreign policy.
“While others have spoken of peace,” he told world leaders, “I have made peace.”

articles.title: North Korea's Kim lauds test of apparent new hypersonic missile
articles.body:
North Korea's Kim Jong Un lauds apparent hypersonic missile test, calls it "incurable headache" for foes
Hong Kong — With his teenage daughter and possible successor by his side, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un watched on Sunday as his country tested a purported new hypersonic weapon designed to evade missile defenses. North Korean state media said Kim had lauded the weapon as an "irresistible force" that would be an "incurable headache" for North Korea's adversaries.
The country's state-run KCNA news agency said the "new weapon" tested on Sunday was "of great significance."
The type of weapon was not specified by the reports, but photographs released by KCNA showed Kim, with his daughter Kim Ju Ae, inspecting a screen with a label reading, "Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory."
Analysts say the title suggests the test was of an upgraded version of an existing North Korean short-range ballistic missile that adds a retrofitted hypersonic glide vehicle. Hypersonic missiles can generally fly lower and faster than conventional rockets, making them more difficult to intercept. North Korea has tested various hypersonic weapons systems since 2021.
They are among the advanced weapons Kim has wanted his country to develop as he seeks to upgrade North Korea's nuclear capabilities.
The test launch on Sunday will come as a blow to South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who is expected to lay out plans to improve relations with Pyongyang at the U.N. General Assembly this week. The two Koreas have remained technically at war since fighting in the Korean War ended in 1953 with a ceasefire agreement rather than a full peace deal.
Lee has proposed dropping South Korea's longstanding demand for Pyongyang to give up its nuclear weapons as a precondition for talks, suggesting instead a freeze on further nuclear weapons testing or development by North Korea, at least initially.
President Trump has also repeatedly expressed interest in meeting with Kim, possibly around the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November. The White House has suggested that talks could be held "without any preconditions."
Mr. Trump met with Kim three times during his first term, but failed to make any progress on the issue of denuclearization. Since then, North Korea has continued to develop its nuclear and conventional weapons programs and is now believed to possess dozens of nuclear warheads.
South Korea's government claims Pyongyang has between 80 and 120 warheads. Mr. Trump recently said the North had 57 nuclear warheads.
The Kim regime has given no indication of interest in a new round of talks with Mr. Trump or with Lee, despite Mr. Trump's move last month to scale back annual military drills with South Korea, which he called "hostile" to Pyongyang.

articles.title: Trump addresses UN General Assembly amid Iran war and tensions with allies – live
articles.body:
Trump defends actions in Iran and Venezuela in UN General Assembly address amid rising tensions with allies – live
Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran and ‘drive them into Hell’ if there isn’t a deal, while also underscoring US policy on Cuba, Mexico, Greenland and AI
Trump opened his speech to the UN by commemorating the nation’s 250th anniversary and focusing not on international issues, but touting his domestic record. Tax cuts, stock market highs, crime rates, and immigration enforcement, to name a few.
He once againframed the war he launched on Iran earlier this year with Israel the same way he has to his domestic audience — as a necessary conflict to addressing a long-ignored threat. The United States, Trump said, had acted to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, while other countries ignored the issue.
Trump then re-issued his threat to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into Hell” if the regime didn’t capitulate and make a deal.” He touted his version of the war: one in which the US had defanged Iran militarily and driven the country to the brink of economic collapse. And hedged by saying he was confident Iran would make a deal after the US midterm elections – an argument he’s made to US voters.
Trump said he was “working closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine” to end the disastrous war. “It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand,” he said. The US president said he had signed into law “a powerful new law” on sanctions, and “if necessary, I will have to use them.” He added: “It’s time to stop the killing.”
Trump defended his administration’s actions in Latin America – including the midnight raid to arrest former Venezuelan president Nicólas Maduro, and the oil deal he struck with his more US-friendly successor, Delcy Rodriguez. “To the victor belong the spoils,” Trump declared, justifying the deal that will funnel a share of the nation’s immense oil wealth into the US treasury.
Defending his drone strikes on boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific, Trump equated the cartels he claims to be fighting with Islamist terrorist organizations. “The cartels are the ISIS of the western Hemisphere – not good people,” he said. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing.”
He accused Mexico of being effectively controlled by the cartels, and said it was “unacceptable” for the US to share a border with a nation under such conditions. “So Mexico must reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity,” Trump said.
Trump also pointed to regime change in Cuba. “My administration is also seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba, where the communist regime is under great pressure, the biggest pressure they’ve ever been under,” he said. “It’s an absolutely failed state. It’s failing.”
Trump said the US has reached “an unprecedented agreement” on Greenland, with the Kingdom of Denmark. He said the deal – to be formally signed shortly after his speech – “gives the US permanent control over security and all of the needs on that territory” and that the US will build two “very major” military bases in Greenland.
Trump said he would reject any calls for a “globalist scheme” to control artificial intelligence, and made an impromptu pitch to world leaders to call the technology “super intelligence” or “SI”. Amid mounting fears over the dangers of AI as some, including leaders in the industry, call for international regulation on the technology, Trump said he would not hinder its growth. He said he believes will be “bigger than the industrial revolution,” and vowed the US would lead on AI. “We’re only going to encourage superintelligence.”
Kamala Harris called Donald Trump’s decision to ban three news organisations from the White House “absolutely abhorrent.”
Answering a reporter’s question following her first appearance of the midterm campaign season, Harris said, “The man is afraid of the voice of the people and that the people understand and know what he’s doing.”
Harris had been speaking at a roundtable on Black maternal health in Michigan alongside Senate-hopeful Abdul El-Sayed.
“He’s trying to stifle the ability of journalists to let the people of America know what’s really going on with their government,” Harris said.
60 Minutes’ blockbuster interview with Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, failed to provide a major ratings boost for the Sunday show, according to audience figures released Tuesday.
Sunday night’s episode of the newsmagazine show drew an average of 6.77m total viewers, the third-smallest audience in the past 25 years for the second episode of a season, adding to a disappointing debut for Bari Weiss, who, as CBS editor-in-chief, rewired the show, firing several high-profile correspondents in the run-up to the new season.
The 59th season debuted on 13 September with an audience down sharply from the 58th season debut, drawing 7.94 million viewers compared with 10 million for last season’s first episode.
Angela Paxton – the Texas state senator who is currently divorcing US Senate-hopeful Ken Paxton – encouraged Republican women to vote the party “even if we’re mad at them,” the Texas Tribune reports.
Paxton said she was divorcing her husband on “biblical grounds,” citing allegations of adultery, in 2025, shortly after her husband announced he would challenge longtime Texas senator John Cornyn. She has not commented on her husband’s race since announcing the divorce, including excluding his name from a list of endorsements in statewide primary races.
According to the Tribune, Angela Paxton addressed a meeting of the Texas Federation of Republican Women on Friday. In a speech titled “The Elephant in the Room” she encouraged the attendees to vote for the party even if they disliked an individual candidate.
“We have more control over that seat and the future when we control the seat — when it’s still in the family, even if we’re mad at them,” she said. “But if we lose it to the other team, the nuances that we want to fix with maybe a certain candidate are nothing compared to what it’s going to take to get it back, right?”
Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer says the shooting of a Venezuelan man by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday “is a direct result of Trump ordering ICE agents to continue deadly traffic stops.”
“ICE must provide a full accounting of what happened, why deadly force was used, and why despite billions in funding agents are still roaming around without cameras and accountability,” Schumer said in a social media post.
After the shooting, Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine.
The supreme court has refused to get involved with a custody dispute between an Alaska surrogate and a California couple whose child was born with a rare and serious heart defect.
On Tuesday, Justice Elena Kagan denied an emergency request from McKenna West, an Alaska nurse and surrogate who had asked the US’s highest court to halt a California court order recognizing the couple, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, as the boy’s legal parents.
In recent weeks, the case has garnered nationwide attention, sparking broader discussions about surrogacy and abortion.
The Cuban delegation withdrew from a session at the UN general assembly after Donald Trump called the country a “failed state”.
“The US government is unable to accept that Cuba is, and has the right to be, a fully independent and sovereign country,” Cuban foreign affairs minister Bruno Rodríguez wrote in a social media post. “The economic blockade, including the energy siege, only threatens Cuba and the rest of the nations. It is an act of genocide and collective punishment. We are a country of peace and we deserve peace.”
As my colleagues Lee Schlenker and Ed Augustin reported last week, “Agrowing cast of Washington and Florida insiders – from billionaire Trump allies and Rubio-linked lobbyists to Cuban exiles – are jockeying for control of the communist-ruled island-nation’s key assets”.
Democratic attorneys general from California and New York have sued the Trump administration over its plans to buy back offshore wind leases as Donald Trump seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.
California attorney general Rob Bonta said he was suing over removal of a project off his state’s coast planned by Chicago-based Invenergy. The Trump administration said in June it was buying back the company’s US offshore wind leases for four wind projects on the east and west coasts.
New York attorney general Letitia James, meanwhile, led seven states in suits seeking to block the Invenergy deal and another proposal with Bluepoint Wind, which agreed in April to end a wind farm under development off the New York and New Jersey coast.
The deals would hand energy companies $1.4bn in taxpayer dollars in exchange for the cancellation of multiple projects. In all, the Trump administration has pledged nearly $4bn to companies to walk away from projects across the country.
Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Donald Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the US president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants.
Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s US midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump and removed a photograph of the congressman and his wife, Erika, posing with the president, the Miami Herald reported.
Until now, Donalds has proudly touted his close ties with the president, running a Republican primary campaign themed largely on Trump’s endorsement, and displaying a large banner on his website advertising his support.
The move comes as Trump’s overall approval rating fell below 30% for the first time, dragged down by dissatisfaction over his handling of the US economy and the Iran war, and Republicans brace for heavy losses in November, including the possible loss of the party’s majorities in the US House of Representatives and Senate.
Republican National Committee sues New Jersey election officials for refusal to turn over voter records
The Republican National Committee has sued top election officials in New Jersey, alleging they failed to produce public voter roll records, including the addresses of noncitizen voters.
The lawsuit follows New Jersey governor Mikie Sherril’s announcement in July that “a software error” in the state’s motor vehicle registration system added 6,600 noncitizens to the state’s voter registration list beginning in 2023. According to the state, 400 votes were cast by noncitizens – although Donald Trump claimed that “thousands of votes” were cast by noncitizens in the state, in an effort to drum up support for his SAVE America Act.
In 2024, Kamala Harris won New Jersey by more than 252,000 votes – meaning that even if all voters were registered as Democrats, which they were not, their votes would not have swung the presidential election.
In Tuesday’s lawsuit, the RNC states that, New Jersey “objected to or denied” several of its records requests “including the request for records of address confirmation notices”.
In July, assistant attorney general for civil rights Harmeet Dhillon wrote to Sherril requesting the “full names, dates of birth, nationalities, residential addresses, and registration dates and locations” of all 6,600 noncitizen voters.
Sherrill has said she will not provide that information. “We now have certain people that, through no fault of their own, have been registered to vote,” she said at a press conference. “It may imperil their immigration status.”
Kamala Harris joined Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed for a roundtable on Black maternal health and mortality in Detroit today. The two spoke with local leaders for more than an hour at Birth Detroit, a Black-led birth center.
The roundtable marked Harris’s first campaign trip of the midterms.
“I’m here to support Dr. El-Sayed because on this subject, I know he will be a champion,” Harris said.
El-Sayed struggled to gain the support of Black voters in his primary election last month. While in Michigan, Harris will also attend a local NAACP event.
The Trump administration will accept 17,500 refugees in fiscal year 2027, CNN reports, citing a copy of the report to Congress.
The vast majority of the refugees are expected to be white South Africans, including Afrikaners. Earlier this year, the administration raised the cap for South African refugees, setting a limit of 17,500 refugees from the country.
“The United States anticipates that Afrikaners from South Africa will fully assimilate into the United States in a manner that preserves taxpayer resources for U.S. citizens and does not anticipate other countries resettling Afrikaners,” the report states.
US president Donald Trump called on all Latin American and Caribbean countries aligned with his administration to designate cartels as narco-terrorists and “apply crushing sanctions” against them.
During a meeting of the Shield of the Americas – an anti-drug cartel coalition formed by 14 Latin American and Caribbean countries governed by rightwing or far-right presidents – Trump said that “for years, cartels have waged war on the people of this hemisphere. Now, we’re waging war on them”.
He added: “So, today, I’m asking all nations in the Shield of the Americas to formally designate narco-terrorists as common threats to stability and apply crushing sanctions against all 24 U.S.-designated foreign terrorist organizations.”
The group, which includes countries such as Argentina, El Salvador and the Dominican Republic, met in New York after Trump said in his speech to the UN General Assembly that “the cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere” and that “like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release”.
In a speech lasting just over 10 minutes to members of the coalition, Trump added: “You probably noticed that the drugs, the fentanyl being delivered by sea, by ocean and sea, it’s down 97 per cent coming into the US” – although many experts have repeatedly pointed out that there is no evidence of fentanyl being produced in or trafficked by sea to the US from South America.
The US president also used the meeting to boast that candidates he had backed had won every election in the region since he took office for a second term.
“There’s been a big shift in your countries, a big shift to the right. That’s a good thing,” said Trump, who particularly celebrated the victory in Colombia of the far-right millionaire former lawyer and businessman Abelardo de la Espriella – who was not present and sent his vice-president instead because he pledged not to leave the country during his four-year term.
“He was a big Trump fan,” said Trump of De la Espriella’s campaign. “All he did was talk about Trump, Trump, Trump. And I said, I like that guy. Let’s endorse him.”
Although the US president said that, after his endorsement, De la Espriella “went from number 10 to number one and won in a landslide”, Trump only endorsed him in the second round, after the Colombian had already won the first round – in which Trump had not backed any candidate.
Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer has criticized Donald Trump’s remarks on Iran at the UN general assembly today, and called for Senate Republicans to join with Democrats in passing a War Powers Resolution this week.
“Only Trump could try to present himself as a peacemaker and then threaten to ‘annihilate’ an entire country in the same breath – that’s what he did at the UN this morning,” Schumer said in a statement.
“This week, Senate Democrats will force another vote on our War Powers Resolution to end this war and get our troops’ out of harm’s way,” he said. “Every Republican who votes against ending the war this week is choosing to pander to the president instead of protecting our troops and our country.”
The United States is withholding a visa for Sudan’s de facto leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan ahead of his scheduled Thursday appearance at the United Nations general assembly, Reuters reports, citing Sudanese and other sources who believe the move is tied to Burhan’s opposition to a US-backed ceasefire proposal.
“We in the Sudanese government express our deep regret because this is a violation of the UN Convention and international law,” a senior Sudanese source told Reuters, adding that Burhan had postponed his trip as he awaited official notice of the visa denial.
The country’s UN ambassador has asked UN secretary-general António Guterres to intervene. Although Burhan, Sudan’s army chief, has attended the UN general assembly before, the country is preparing to have foreign minister Mohieldin Salem stand in for him on Thursday.
In a statement, UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told Reuters that Guterres is “deeply concerned that a visa has reportedly not yet been issued.”
Speaking at the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Donald Trump said his diplomatic representatives – real estate investor Steve Witkoff and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner - had “a very productive meeting today” with Iranian mediators.
While addressing a meeting of the Gulf Cooperation Council – a security alliance comprised of leaders from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman – Trump suggested his team could reach a peace deal with Iran. Trump has claimed that the war with Iran, which began in February, would only last a few weeks.
According to Iranian state media, the country’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi met Witkoff to discuss conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump's FBI killed corruption probe into Susan Collins' campaign: report
The FBI under Trump killed an anti-corruption probe into Susan Collins, the Republican senator from Maine, stemming from a convicted former defense contracting executive’s claims that he’d paid off Collins’ campaign in exchange for government contracts, ProPublica reported Tuesday.
The report by ProPublica presents evidence that Kao contributed campaign funds in return for Collins steering funds toward Kao’s company, Navatek. Kao, facing criminal charges, began sharing details on an alleged scheme with the FBI to skirt campaign finance laws to contribute to Collins’ campaign treasury, ProPublica reported.
Annie Clark, Collins’ deputy chief of staff, denied the allegations in a post to social media.
“The seven-year-old allegations made against Senator Collins and her staff in this piece are categorically false,” Clark wrote. She said that Collins’ campaign cooperated fully with the FBI, and that ProPublica was amplifying false and “outlandish” allegations Kao made while trying deflect blame for his own crimes. “There have never been any allegations of wrongdoing by the Collins for Senator campaign, and the campaign was never the target of the FBI investigation.”
Trump strikes warm tone in meeting with UK prime minister
Andrew Sparrow
Trump also met earlier this afternoon with the the United Kingdom’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, with whom he appeared to enjoy a solid rapport – a divergence from his at-times testy relationship with Burnham’s predecessor in the role, Keir Starmer.
“I think he’s going to be a great prime minister,” Trump said of Burnham. “I think he’s got a lot of assets on his side.”
Trump added: “We talked about everything from Rolls-Royce to energy, immigration. We covered a lot.”
One point of tension in an otherwise cordial exchange: the Chagos Islands deal, a proposal by Keir Starmer’s goverment to give Mauritius sovereignty over the Chagos Islands, on condition that the US and the UK can continue to operate the Diego Garcia military base there for at least another 99 years.
“I don’t support it,” Trump said. “I think it’s a terrible deal.”
At one point the relationship between Trump and Starmer was good. But it worsened as Starmer started to criticize Trump publicly on issues like his proposal to annex Greenland, and his claim British troops avoided frontline action in Afghanistan. And the full rupture came when Keir Starmer refused to allow the US to use British airbases for attacks against Iran at the start of the war.
Members of US delegation met Iranian leadership at UN, Trump says
During a press conference alongside Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump said some members of his team met today with the Iranian delegation, a meeting that he said lasted three hours and “went very well.”
Trump left the exact nature of the exchange – what was discussed, and what progress, if any, was made toward a deal – unclear, but said it was a “a very good meeting.” He then repeated his threat delivered to the assembled world leaders in an address earlier that morning that Iran had to choose between “potential greatness or obliteration.”
“They had a very good meeting, and they have another one scheduled in the near future,” Trump said, teasing future conversations with Iran.
Steve Witkoff, Trump’s special envoy to the Middle East, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law-turned-Middle East diplomat, sat alongside the president. Both declined to share specifics of the meeting.
“I feel very good right now,” Witkoff said when asked how he felt after the initial meeting.
“How will you feel tomorrow?” a reporter pressed him.
Trump endorses a US embargo on diesel exports in conversation with Zelenskyy
President Trump appeared to support the increasingly loud calls from some members of his party to halt the export of US diesel fuel, whose skyrocketing price has begun to ripple out through the American economy and stung Republicans ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
“I’ve called for that too, I’ve said, ‘let’s not send out the diesel’,” Trump said, when asked about the outcry from his fellow Republicans.
He then turned to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, sitting at his side, who said the Trump administration is evaluating the feasibility of a full or partial plan. Trump declined to share a timeline for when such a ban could come down.
The subject was raised after a reporter mentioned Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, which Trump was quick to point out had damaged global diesel supplies. (The conflict between the US and Iran, which Trump launched in February alongside Israel, has also strangled global energy markets.)
“It is a serious hit on the Russians,” Trump said. “It’s also a very serious hit on the price of diesel.”

articles.title: North Korea tests missile with maneuvering glide warhead
articles.body:
- North Korea fired two ballistic missiles from Wonsan on Sunday, with the second flying more than 600 km (370 miles), South Korea's military said.
- North Korean state media called it a test of a "new type of weapon," which analysts said appeared to involve a hypersonic glide vehicle warhead.
North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area toward the sea on Sunday, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said, with the second missile flying more than 600 km (370 miles).
Kim Jong Un oversaw the launch, and North Korean state media called it a test of a “new type of weapon.”
South Korea said the first missile launched around 3 p.m. local time and flew about 450 km (280 miles). The second launched roughly three hours later, at 5:50 p.m., and flew farther and higher, reaching an altitude of about 70 km (43 miles) compared with roughly 60 km (37 miles) for the first, according to flight data broadcast on North Korean state television and cited by open-source analysts. South Korean and U.S. authorities said they were still analyzing the missiles’ exact specifications.
North Korea’s Missile Administration said the test marked “a significant step in the technological development of its weapons systems,” and Kim said the advance would give an adversary “an incurable headache.” A monitor shown in North Korean state media footage was labeled “Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory,” identifying the missile by name; North Korea did not publicly confirm what kind of warhead it carried. NK News, a Seoul-based outlet that tracks North Korea, said the projectile appeared to be an upgraded missile fitted with a hypersonic glide vehicle, a maneuverable warhead that separates from its booster and glides toward its target rather than following a fixed ballistic arc.
State media footage showed a flight-path graphic on a command-center screen that tracked the second missile through what appeared to be a pull-up maneuver, a sharp change in trajectory during flight that missile defenses have a harder time predicting. South Korean expert Chang Young-keun, cited by the Korea Herald, said the system paired a KN-23-style missile body with a hypersonic glide vehicle terminal section built to penetrate missile defenses while striking targets hundreds of kilometers away. He said it looked like a refinement of a system North Korea first tested last October rather than an entirely new weapon.
North Korea has tested hypersonic glide vehicles since September 2021, when it first flew the wedge-shaped warhead later associated with the Hwasong-8 missile. It has since tested at least two other missile types carrying similar warheads, the Hwasong-12B and the solid-fueled Hwasong-16B. In a January 2025 test of the Hwasong-16B, Japan estimated the missile flew about 1,100 km (680 miles) with an apogee near 100 km (62 miles); North Korea claimed a longer range and two separate apogees, an initial climb followed by a lower secondary peak consistent with a glide phase.
Sunday’s launches were North Korea’s 15th and 16th ballistic missile launches of the year, spread across nine test events, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said. That is roughly triple last year’s total of at least five missiles across four events, he said, calling the regional security situation “increasingly severe.” Japan lodged a formal protest, and South Korea’s National Security Council condemned the launch and called on North Korea to halt missile activity, saying it violated United Nations Security Council resolutions. The launches came about a week after North Korea’s previous test, on Sept. 12, and days after Pyongyang rejected a UN resolution demanding it halt its nuclear program.

articles.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine kill three as Zelenskyy in US for UN summit
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Ukraine kill three as Zelenskyy in US for UN summit
Overnight missile and drone attacks hit several Ukrainian regions as world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly.
Russian forces have launched widespread attacks targeting industrial sites and critical energy infrastructure across several regions of Ukraine, killing at least three people and knocking out power to nearly 100,000 residents, Ukrainian officials said.
The strikes overnight hit industrial facilities simultaneously in the Dnipropetrovsk region, including Dnipro, Pavlohrad and Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, regional Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram on Tuesday.

Three people were killed and six others were wounded in Dnipro, where missiles, drones and artillery heavily damaged business and warehouse premises, Hanzha said.
Ukraine’s air force said Moscow’s overnight barrage involved 212 drones, four cruise missiles, and an unspecified number of Oniks antiship and ballistic missiles.
The strikes also damaged energy infrastructure. An attack on a power facility left nearly 100,000 consumers without electricity in the northern region of Chernihiv, while in the Poltava region, Governor Vitalii Diakivnych said a “massive” Russian attack hit an industrial enterprise and a critical infrastructure facility.
The Russian Ministry of Defence confirmed its forces carried out major strikes, stating it hit industrial and military facilities, the fuel and energy sector, port infrastructure and sea vessels operating for the Ukrainian military.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drones targeted Russia’s Samara region along the Volga River, killing one person and injuring four, according to the local governor. The region hosts critically important facilities, including oil refineries.
The Russian Defence Ministry said its air defence units intercepted and destroyed 297 Ukrainian drones across various regions overnight.
Diplomatic push in New York
The attacks come as Zelenskyy arrived in New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where talks on ending the war are set to be high on the agenda as nearly 130 heads of state gather.
The Ukrainian president wrote on X that a “drone deal” was ready to be signed to bolster air defence and secure funding for the war effort.
“Of course, Ukraine’s number one priority is bringing peace closer and protecting the lives of our people,” Zelenskyy posted. “There are concrete security proposals and de-escalation measures that could bring the end of the war closer. We are working to strengthen air defence and ensure sufficient financing for Ukraine.”
He said, “Around 20 meetings are planned, including with the US president, European leaders, US senators and members of the House of Representatives, heads of international organisations, leading American companies and think tanks.”
Zelenskyy met French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday and is likely to meet US President Donald Trump on Tuesday.
Earlier, Macron also met Trump, after which he said the two countries agreed to work together to secure a moratorium on strikes targeting energy networks and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine. Both Zelenskyy and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov are set to address the UNGA later this week.

articles.title: Iran, AI and the ICC: Trump makes threats, touts policies at UN General Assembly
articles.body:
Iran, AI and the ICC: Trump makes threats, touts policies at UN General Assembly
US President Donald Trump launched a full-throated defence of the deeply unpopular US-Israeli war against Iran before the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, claiming that Washington would reach a deal with Tehran after the upcoming US midterm elections. Trump also rejected the idea of global regulation of artificial intelligence, said the government of Cuba would soon "fall", and urged member countries of the International Criminal Court to "resign".
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
US President Donald Trump said Tuesday he was deciding whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate" the country in a bombastic 37-minute speech to the United Nations that appeared tailored to war-weary American voters.
The 80-year-old president's threat came after repeated claims that under him the United States is successfully confronting its adversaries and reshaping the world order to its own advantage.
Read moreUN Live: 'Nobody with a conscience can close their eyes to what is happening in Gaza', Erdogan says
Since returning to office last year for a second term, Trump has sent shockwaves through the global order, joining Israel to attack Iran, ordering an armed raid on Venezuela that seized the country's president and threatening to annex Greenland by military force.
"While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them," Trump told the room full of world leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York.
Despite claiming credit as a peacemaker, Trump delivered a jarring warning as he sought to justify the nearly seven-month war against Iran, which he claimed was launched to stop Tehran acquiring nuclear weapons.
"I have a big decision to make – will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country?" Trump said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival?"
Trump spoke less than a week after a UN fact-finding mission said it had reasonable grounds to believe US forces committed war crimes in two strikes on Iran, including one that killed scores of children in a primary school in the southern city of Minab.
Trump reiterated that he believed Iran would "make a deal right after" the US midterm elections in November – in which his Republican party faces losing control of Congress, at least partly due to high fuel prices caused by the unpopular war.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
'Military might'
Much of the rest of his speech was dedicated to proclaiming his own achievements in making the United States the "most powerful country in the world".
Trump threatened to use the "unmatched military might" of the US to secure Washington's interests in Latin America, and said the Communist-run island of Cuba would soon "fall".
Cuba has suffered repeated nationwide blackouts after the US imposed a devastating fuel blockade on the Caribbean nation in January, leaving millions of people without power.
Members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the hall as Trump referenced his pressure campaign against the country.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
He also hailed a deal with Greenland under which he said Washington would build two bases in the Arctic territory. Trump was signing the deal with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland on the sidelines of the UN.
The Greenland deal has sparked bitter divisions within long-term US alliances including NATO and revived fears that under Trump Washington is no longer a reliable partner.
The volatile US president also renewed his attack on what he claimed were "far-left globalist" bodies, including the United Nations itself and the International Criminal Court, which he urged other countries to boycott.
'Super intelligence'
Trump also rejected calls for international supervision of artificial intelligence, calling them a "globalist scheme" to control the new technology.
The US president announced that the US government would henceforth use the term "super intelligence" rather than "artificial intelligence" in its communications, and said he hoped the world would follow suit.
"It sounds much better," he added, claiming the term was "much more accurate".
Trump also dismissed warnings from AI safety advocates, comparing them to warnings about climate change, whose human causes are affirmed by the overwhelming consensus of the scientific community.
"Every major new technology brings challenges, and super intelligence is no exception," he said.
Ahead of the week of meetings and speeches in New York, leaders of more than 20 countries urged binding safety measures for advanced artificial intelligence, warning that the technology's development could outpace the ability to control it.
AI superpowers China and the United States are not signatories.
Watch moreAI-pocalypse? Tech leaders, politicians clash over development slowdown
Trump told the UN that the "United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control ... artificial intelligence."
UN chief Antonio Guterres, meanwhile, called for the US and China to start a dialogue on the technology's future akin to US-Soviet engagement at the height of the Cold War.
"Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation," Guterres said in his address to the assembly.
"At a pivotal moment during the Cold War, strategic rivals came to recognise the need to manage shared existential risks."
Trump's speech to the world body was perhaps less fiery than last year's, which was characterised by Trump's extraordinary accusations of UN sabotage.
Those claims were sparked when an escalator in New York briefly stopped working and the teleprompter glitched. This year Trump ascended the escalator with wife Melania without a hitch, and appeared to read his speech faithfully from the teleprompter.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Trump’s Message to Putin: ‘Settle the War’
articles.body:
Speaking at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), US President Donald Trump urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war against Ukraine and said he was prepared to use newly granted legislative powers to impose tariffs of up to 100% on Russian energy buyers.
Trump made the remarks on the first day of the high-level general debate on Tuesday, Sept. 22. The annual assembly opened on Sept. 8, and is scheduled to conclude on Sept. 28.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ahead of his UN address, when a reporter asked what message he had for Putin, he simply said: “Settle the war.”
His comments came ahead of a scheduled meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who previously expressed hope for using the venue to meet with Trump to restore the diplomatic momentum gained by the visits from senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow then Kyiv earlier this month.
“Last week, in honor of Senator Lindsey Graham, I signed a powerful new law passed by Congress, providing me with enormous new tariff authorities,” Trump said.
“And, if necessary, I will have to use them. It’s time to stop the killing,” he continued.
Diplomacy resumes in New York
Trump spoke early on the first day, following Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in keeping with the tradition under which Brazil opens the debate and the US – being the host country – speaks next.
French President Emmanuel Macron, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham were among the other leaders scheduled to address the assembly during its opening day
Hungary-Ukraine Diplomatic Relations Strain Further as Magyar Likens C8 to Village Football
During his UN address, Trump expressed confidence that Washington could help broker an end to the war, although he did not announce a ceasefire or any negotiating framework between Kyiv and Moscow.
“We’re working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done,” Trump said, according to Clash Reports.
“It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand. They’ve had it,” he continued.
The president presented his approach as one of direct intervention rather than prolonged diplomacy. “I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester. They only become harder to solve,” Trump said.
However, no further details about Washington’s resolution to bridge the fundamental differences between Kyiv and Moscow had been offered.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that there had been no progress in negotiations, although Moscow hoped trilateral talks would eventually resume.
In July, Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin no longer planned to return any occupied Ukrainian territory as part of a future peace deal. Instead, Putin reportedly intended to keep occupied areas of the Sumy and Kharkiv regions as permanent buffer zones, while continuing his push to seize all of the Donetsk region.
Kyiv categorically rejects any settlement requiring it to surrender territory and maintains that a peace agreement must respect Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders and sovereignty.
Renewed US mediation earlier in September
Trump’s most recent speech follows a renewed US mediation earlier in September.
Special US envoys Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5 during talks lasting more than three hours, then traveled to Kyiv on Sept. 6 for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital as Washington’s intermediaries.
Prospects for a direct Trump-Zelensky meeting in New York initially appeared uncertain.
As of Sept. 19, Zelensky was absent from the list of bilateral meetings publicly outlined by US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, while two senior Ukrainian officials told Suspilne that no meeting had been finalized.
The situation changed following a Sunday, Sept. 20 telephone discussion between the two leaders, who agreed to meet with “ideas for de-escalation steps.” By Tuesday, the bilateral talks had been added to Trump’s schedule, with Reuters reporting that Zelensky was among at least 11 leaders the US president planned to meet during UNGA.
The discussions are expected to center on air defense – particularly US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapons Ukraine relies on to successfully deter Russian ballistic missiles – as well as energy and security.
Kyiv is urgently seeking additional protection ahead of its fifth winter of war, as the country prepares for intensified Russian attacks against critical infrastructure, such as heating, power and water supplies.

articles.title: The Narrow Path to a Xi-Trump AI Deal
articles.body:
When Donald Trump arrived in Beijing in May, Xi Jinping was already on the offensive. The Chinese leader wasted zero time in rebuking his U.S. counterpart over arms sales to Taiwan directly warning that simmering tensions over the self-ruling island could ultimately cause the superpowers to “enter into conflict.”
Trump acquiesced. He delayed a $14 billion arms package to Taiwan, said future weapons would be discussed as a “very good negotiating chip” with Beijing, questioned the island’s sovereignty as something “nobody knows how to define,” and stressed that he was not looking to fight a war “9,500 miles away”—all without securing any apparent reduction in Chinese military pressure in return.
While this response alarmed many in democratic Taiwan, many people around the globe hope that Xi can prove similarly persuasive on another issue of grave importance when he travels to the White House on Sept 24: artificial intelligence.
“Taiwan is not a priority anymore,” Wang Yiwei, director of the Institute of International Affairs at Beijing's Renmin University, says of Xi’s impending visit. “The priority is definitely AI.”
In recent days, warnings from a whistleblower researcher and reports of rogue agent swarms have intensified fears of a doomsday scenario born of unbridled AI development. On Sept. 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier calling for embedded independent evaluators, common safety standards among democracies, and eventually verifiable global coordination to slow dangerous frontier-AI development. OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk also voiced broad support for slowing frontier development.
However, one major skeptic is Trump, who responded on Truth Social that “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” Moreover, he insisted that “President Xi, of China, just announced that China will be doing absolutely nothing to stand in the way of AI, or its future.”
That characterization is misleading. China regulates AI more stringently than most other countries, and already enforces AI security guidance, ethics review requirements, and binding obligations on consumer AI services. Xi has also publicly called for legal, technical, and ethical guardrails that keep AI under human control (albeit while resisting restrictions that could impede China’s technological rise). “We should strengthen risk-awareness and ensure that AI is secure and controllable,” he told the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai on July 17.
The hope among safety advocates is that Xi and Trump might strike a deal on AI. While Trump’s first term was anchored in antipathy to China, he posed a notably different tone in Beijing, calling Xi “a man I respect greatly” and telling him that “it’s an honor to be your friend.” Although that cordiality does not erase the national competition that makes either side hesitant to constrain its technological development, it may put narrower cooperation on the table.
Certainly, the moment is ripe to build a framework built on competition, cooperation, and strict guardrails. Beyond economic rivalry, both Washington and Beijing share an urgent interest in mitigating catastrophic miscalculations, particularly surrounding AI integration into defense architectures and nuclear command and control systems.
Trump also enters the summit under pressure, with soaring energy prices from the Iran war adding to voter discontent ahead of the midterms. “Trump needs a win more than Xi does,” says Jonathan Sullivan, head of China programs at the Asia Research Institute at the University of Nottingham.
Still, Xi’s motivations require clear-eyed scrutiny. Last week, Chen Yixin, China’s Minister of State Security, published an article in China Cyberspace Magazine that expounded upon the opportunities and challenges of AI. The top “risk,” he said, was “political security, institutional security, and ideological security.”
While the deeply paranoid Chinese Communist Party (CCP) won’t allow its people to access Google or Facebook, it cannot countenance AI exhibiting the kind of autonomy that was on display in July. That month, a “swarm” of OpenAI agents circumvented sandbox controls, communicated through unauthorized channels, gained access to AI platform Hugging Face, compromised credentials, and accessed internal datasets while trying to game evaluations. It’s enough to give a regime built on control pause.
But while China’s motivations may be driven as much by safeguarding party control as by addressing broader risks to humanity, these objectives can overlap. “If they go beyond bilateral competition and address so many concerns about AI development, that would show the co-leadership of China and the U.S.,” says Wang. “Not just two superpowers, but also two civilizations.”
However, any agreement requires overcoming profound distrust. Even as Amodei argued for pacing frontier AI development, he framed it in terms of competing with China, whose “lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world.” On that score, he advocated stronger export controls on advanced semiconductors, a crackdown on chip smuggling, and greater efforts to prevent Chinese companies from “distilling” the capabilities of Western models.
The contradiction of calling for a slowdown while talking up the “race” narrative wasn’t lost on critics (who also pointed out that Anthropic could temper its own research without external intervention). Others suggested that because cheap, open-weight Chinese AI models are among the chief rivals to Anthropic’s proprietary models, its CEO’s call to crack down on Chinese AI development could be seen as commercially motivated rather than altruistic—especially as the firm eyes a potential record-breaking IPO that could value the company at $2 trillion.
Indeed, China was quick to leap on Amodei’s essay as an example of “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition [that] will only hamper efforts toward sound global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said last week. A flurry of strident op-eds in state media followed, with the CCP mouthpiece Global Times calling the essay a “‘Cold War script’ for the AI field.”
Amodei has long been a bête noire in Beijing for painting AI as a tussle between democracies and autocracies that casts China as the principal threat. “If there's ever a proposal that requires Chinese buy-in, the last person on earth that would be a good salesman is Dario Amodei,” says Ryan Hass, an expert in U.S.-China relations at the Brookings Institution.
But Amodei’s framing of AI as a zero-sum contest is far from an outlier—it is shared by a large chunk of the Trump administration. “There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sept. 8. “If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter.”
A grand bargain to slow AI development is unlikely, and grievances over distillation or export controls could stall negotiations. But experts see room for narrower cooperation. Both countries face threats from non-state actors using AI to sabotage infrastructure, mount cyberattacks, or create biological weapons, argues Alvin W. Graylin, a digital fellow at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. Sharing information about those threats could benefit both sides.
When Bessent met Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and chief trade negotiator Li Chenggang on Sunday to thrash out summit objectives, he reportedly proposed a formal AI dialogue and a mechanism for each side to notify the other of AI incidents which threaten national security. Modest a measure it may be, it would be an important step towards avoiding some of the worst risks, says Scott Singer, a fellow and co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “I wouldn’t take these small but critical steps for granted.”
Such a channel could help either side respond during a crisis, and reduce the risk of mistaking a non-state actor or rogue AI as an act of aggression. Reminiscent of the “red phone” that connected Washington to Moscow during the Cold War, experts have floated the idea of a literal fax machine to avoid mistranslations.
To be sure, Beijing has not publicly endorsed the proposal. Even if it does, important questions remain. What, for example, would classify a national security threat? Its effectiveness would also depend on whether governments learned of serious incidents. OpenAI only reported its agents' autonomous cyberattack after Hugging Face, the target of the attack, reported the breach to the FBI. Independent researchers have since uncovered other apparent instances of OpenAI agents compromising websites.
Beyond the proposed channel, Bessent has said the two countries have agreed to establish a recurring dialogue. Who will staff those talks, and how often they will meet, remains unclear. More than two years elapsed between the last official AI dialogue and Sunday’s meeting.
With the stakes quickly rising, Singer says another prolonged hiatus from the negotiating table could prove disastrous. “Who knows where we’re going to be in June 2027,” he says with respect to AI development. “This cannot go off the rails.”

articles.title: Saudis may seek help from Israel as current alliances prove insufficient against Houthis - analysis
articles.body:
The sharp escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has raised concerns that the confrontation could spread further across the region, with Washington worried that the conflict could intensify and potentially lead the Houthis to resume direct attacks on Israel, diplomatic officials told Maariv on Tuesday.
The officials said the key question is whether the situation can be brought under control or whether the confrontation will continue to escalate. Among the regional consequences being considered is the possibility that the Houthis could again try to attack Israel directly, as they did last year.
The concerns come after the US State Department updated its security guidance for American citizens in the Middle East, warning that the military confrontation between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia could escalate rapidly. The US Embassy in Israel also issued an alert urging citizens to remain vigilant and consider the possibility of flight disruptions, airspace closures, and transportation disruptions.
Diplomatic officials stressed that the updated and expanded warnings should not necessarily be seen as a sign that immediate developments are expected. The wording, they said, also reflects the administration's responsibility to warn American citizens in the region and make clear the seriousness of the situation should the confrontation intensify.
The warnings come against the backdrop of the latest escalation in the confrontation. Saudi Arabia confirmed that the Houthis launched a ballistic missile toward Riyadh, which was intercepted by the Saudi air defense system.
It was the first time the Saudi capital had been targeted since the current wave of escalation began. Residents reported hearing an explosion, and smoke was later seen near Riyadh's airport. No casualties or damage were reported.
The Houthis claimed they attacked "sensitive targets" in Riyadh with missiles and drones, as well as facilities belonging to oil giant Aramco in Yanbu. Saudi Arabia said it had also thwarted attempts to strike civilian infrastructure in Yanbu, Taif, Baish, and the Farasan Islands. Houthi claims that Aramco facilities were hit have not been verified.
Saudis divide efforts between defending territory, Red Sea shipping
The wave of attacks has forced Saudi Arabia to divide its efforts between defending cities and infrastructure from missiles and drones, securing energy facilities, and protecting shipping routes in the Red Sea.
In recent months, the Houthis have expanded their attacks on Saudi Arabia and shipping in the region, and in July they declared a naval blockade against the kingdom. Any disruption to traffic through the Bab al-Mandab Strait could significantly increase the economic and strategic cost of the confrontation.
Amid the tensions, US President Donald Trump returned to the White House from Camp David earlier than planned. No official explanation was given for the schedule change, and no confirmation links his early return to developments in the Middle East.
The return came as discussions were underway in Washington over the desired extent of US involvement in the confrontation. US media reported that options for action against the Houthis were examined while Trump was at Camp David, but no US decision to launch a strike was announced.
Washington has so far refrained from direct military intervention alongside Saudi Arabia in the current round of fighting and has not agreed to Riyadh's request to take military action against the Houthis.
Israel is closely monitoring developments. Israeli officials believe the pressure facing Saudi Arabia could also affect Riyadh's diplomatic calculations.
"Such an escalation could actually help the Abraham Accords," the officials said.
Israeli officials: Saudis recognizing alliances insufficient for Houthi threat
According to the officials, the Saudis are under pressure and are discovering that the relationships and alliances they have built are not currently providing a complete response to the threat. If the Houthi threat intensifies and the assistance the kingdom receives from its allies remains limited, they assess that Israeli capabilities could carry greater weight in the eyes of the Saudi leadership.
Saudi Arabia has been working in recent weeks to secure outside assistance. According to reports, amid a shortage of interceptors, it has requested air-defense assistance from France, the UK, Pakistan, and Egypt.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman also traveled to Cairo and, according to the reports, sought Egyptian support against the Houthis.
Security cooperation among Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan is also being tested by developments on the ground.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Ankara was prepared to assist with Saudi military needs under the defense agreement among the three countries. Pakistan has so far not joined military action against the Houthis.
The gap between Riyadh's security needs and the assistance it is actually receiving is at the heart of the Israeli assessment. Israeli officials point in this context to the experience and capabilities Israel has accumulated in intelligence and air defense against the Houthis.
As the campaign continues, they assess that those capabilities could also become part of Saudi Arabia's broader considerations.

articles.title: Ukraine’s new interceptor drone moves toward mass production after first kills against jet-powered Russian drones that fly like cruise missiles
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Wild Hornets says its new STING-family interceptor drone has destroyed about ten Russian Geran-4 jet drones and several Geran-5s—technically also drones but ones whose jet engines make them functionally small cruise missiles—in limited deployment over recent days, according to an interview with a company representative published by NV on 22 September. The company says it plans to begin mass production within about a month after completing combat tests.
Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-powered Shahed-type drones this year. At least twenty firms were already racing to field interceptors by early September. Their higher speeds can cut the reaction time for Ukrainian mobile fire groups from about a minute to as little as six seconds. Two companies have completed combat tests, and 67 companies are working on interceptors, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
A new product, not an upgrade
Wild Hornets told NV it began work on jet interception in early 2026 and described the new interceptor as an entirely new product rather than an upgrade of the existing STING design. To handle the faster targets, the company developed a remote-control system called Hornet Vision Ctrl that lets experienced pilots operate interceptors across multiple sectors at once—the same system now used against jet-powered Gerans.
"We are working on that, but right now we are focused above all on creating a cheap, mass-producible, and simple-to-use means of countering jet Shaheds," the company told NV, answering a question about expectations that Russia could field mass jet missiles at 700–800 km/h by winter.
The company said it knows of no fully automatic interception system proven in combat and that its own AI integration is aimed at assisting the operator.
The jet-powered threat
Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat said in August that the use of jet-powered drones had increased roughly fivefold in July compared with June. The Geran-5 can reach speeds of up to 600 km/h and carry a warhead of roughly 90 kg, according to specifications published on HUR's War & Sanctions website. The new jet Shaheds run on turbojets from a single Chinese company. Iran, which originally armed Russia with Shaheds, now wants the jet-powered Geran-5 remake back.
Earlier this month, a new interceptor successfully hit a jet-powered Shahed during testing, but "some aspects of controlling the interceptor still need to be refined," Zelenskyy said. Days later, he showed footage of a Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) interceptor destroying a jet-powered Shahed during a military counterintelligence operation. The SBU said it was the first footage showing the destruction of a jet-powered Shahed.
