articles.title: F-16 Crashes in Germany; Pilot Successfully Ejects
articles.body:
A U.S. Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon crashed on a local mission in Germany on Sept. 22.
The pilot ejected safely and is receiving medical care, Air Force officials said. The fighter was assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing at Spangdahlem Air Base. The jet went down on base property in the Eifel region of western Germany.
The wing said in a statement the cause of the crash is under investigation and emergency personnel are at the scene of the crash. The jet went down around 2:30 p.m. local time.
This is the second F-16 crash for the Air Force in five days—a Viper belonging to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing crashed during a training mission in Michigan on Sept. 17. The pilot in that crash ejected safely as well.
The 52nd Fighter Wing has one squadron of F-16s that specializes in the “Wild Weasel” mission of suppressing enemy air defenses. The U.S. military has deployed fighters from the unit to the Middle East twice during the seven-month conflict with Iran. Forward deployments typically consist of a dozen fighter jets, and Spangdahlem has over two dozen F-16s that comprise the 52nd Fighter Wing’s sole fighter squadron, the 480th Fighter Squadron. The 480th is permanently based at Spangdahlem as part of U.S. Air Forces in Europe.
Images posted to social media and captured by local press show a charred hunk of the F-16, including what appears to be its engine, amid a wide debris field. Black smoke billowed over the base as emergency personnel responded to the scene.

articles.title: Trump is expected to press Zelensky to accept a Russia-Ukraine energy truce at their NYC meeting
articles.body:
Trump is expected to press Zelensky to accept a Russia-Ukraine energy truce at their NYC meeting
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky will meet with U.S. President Donald Trump in New York on the evening of September 22. According to The Guardian, Trump is expected to press Zelensky at the meeting to agree to an energy ceasefire with Russia.
The Ukrainian and U.S. leaders spoke by phone on Sunday, September 20. Sources told the Financial Times that their conversation was about “diesel, diesel, diesel.” The next day, Trump discussed the idea of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine with French President Emmanuel Macron. Macron called the conversation “very constructive” and promised to raise the issue at his meeting with Zelensky as well.
Trump is unhappy with Ukrainian strikes targeting Russia’s diesel production and has already asked Zelensky to halt the attacks. On September 13, he explicitly blamed Kyiv for rising fuel prices, emphasizing that the war between Russia and Ukraine — not the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran — was responsible.
As early as September 14, Trump said Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure. Sources told the Financial Times that the announcement was premature. People familiar with the Kremlin’s position told the newspaper that Putin would not agree to such a deal because attacks on energy facilities during the winter could give him additional leverage over Kyiv.
Since then, Russia has struck energy infrastructure in Kyiv, Odesa, Zaporizhzhia, and the Sumy and Odesa regions. An employee of Zaporizhzhiaoblenergo was killed in one of the strikes. After Russia’s overnight attack on September 22, residents of seven Ukrainian regions were left without electricity.
Ukraine, in turn, has attacked the Syzran, Yaroslavl, Moscow, and Kuybyshev oil refineries. Trump said the repeated attacks had caused Russia to lose control of its diesel industry — and that “The whole World suffers” as a result.
The Kremlin called an energy ceasefire “a good idea” but said keeping refineries operating safely and increasing production of petroleum products would not solve “global problems” — lifting sanctions on shipments and ensuring the safety of tankers were far more important.
Zelensky said Russia and Ukraine see the problem completely differently: Moscow is thinking about the oil and gas trade, while Kyiv is thinking about electricity in people’s homes. He proposed that Russia “put on the table” a list of facilities to be covered by the ceasefire. On Monday, Zelensky listed the targets Russia must stop striking:
Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part. Solutions are possible.
Zelensky and Trump are scheduled to meet at 8:15 p.m. Moscow time. According to Reuters, the outcome of the talks is difficult to predict. The news agency pointed to the two leaders’ public meeting in Washington in February 2025, which ended in a heated exchange broadcast live.
The war in photos: Kramatorsk
Russia attacked Kramatorsk on Monday, September 21. Donetsk regional police said Russian forces struck the city with KAB-250 aerial bombs, Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, and drones. One person was killed, and seven others were injured, including two children. Eight apartment buildings and 17 private homes were damaged. The photographs show the aftermath of the strikes.

articles.title: Zelensky Condemns Delistings of Russian Oligarchs in Western Sanctions
articles.body:
During his meeting with European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen, President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the delistment of Russian oligarchs in the Western sanctions, arguing that such move would undermine pressure on Moscow while Russian missile and drone barrage continues across Ukraine.
Detailing Tuesday’s meeting in a statement on Telegram, Zelensky said the two leaders also discussed Ukraine’s financial stability for this and the upcoming year, including the EU’s €90 billion (roughly $103 billion) loan package intended to support Kyiv’s defense needs.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“At a time when Russia is carrying out brutal attacks against our people – and even now, during the General Assembly, air-raid alerts are sounding in many regions because of drones and ballistic missiles,” Zelensky said, “signals about lifting sanctions on certain Russian oligarchs appear suicidal and counterproductive.”
Financial support on the agenda
The EU disbursed €3.3 billion (roughly $3.7 billion) to Ukraine for the procurement of missiles and drones on Friday, Sept. 18, following a phone call by Zelensky and Von der Leyen just a day earlier.
Brussels said it was prepared to use remaining funds from the EU’s SAFE defense program – an EU defense financing initiative worth €150 billion (about $172 billion) – to launch additional EU-Ukraine defense projects.
Hungary-Ukraine Diplomatic Relations Strain Further as Magyar Likens C8 to Village Football
During the same call, the leaders agreed to meet in New York during the 81st United Nations General Assembly’s (UNGA) high-level week, which runs from Tuesday, Sept. 22 through Monday, Sept. 28.
Their talks reflect Kyiv’s effort to secure continuing financial and military assistance as it faces pressure on public finances and repeated Russian air attacks.
“We are grateful for the decision on the EU’s €90 billion (approximately €103 billion) loan, and Ukraine is fulfilling the obligations associated with it in order to cover the budget deficit as much as possible,” Zelensky said following the meeting on Tuesday.
“We agreed that our teams will also explore other avenues of financial support,” he continued.
The broader EU budget picture remains central to those discussions. Member states have still not raised objections to a proposed €100 billion ($115 billion) Ukraine allocation in the bloc’s next seven-year budget, covering 2028 through 2034.
The EU leaders are expected to consider the long-term framework at an Oct. 15-16 summit in Brussels.
Latvia drops veto on oligarch deal
Earlier Tuesday, the EU agreed to extend its Russian sanctions after Latvia dropped its opposition to the new version that would delist two Russian oligarchs – Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, both closely connected to Russian President Vladimir Putin and Moscow’s wartime effort.
Latvia dropped its veto only hours before the current sanctions expire on Tuesday night.
The EU ambassadors failed to agree on extending the Western sanctions for the second time after France joined Slovakia in demanding changes to the list of sanctioned individuals on Sept. 11.
The sanctions, imposed on the blacklisted individuals from 2022, were temporarily extended for a week on Sept. 14 when negotiations reached a deadlock.
The EU officials ultimately agreed to delist Usmanov and Fridman in exchange for a longer, three-year extension instead of the usual half-year or one-year extensions.

articles.title: Understanding Trump's Deal With Denmark—and What It Means for Greenland's Sovereignty
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday signed a deal on the security of the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland, in a bid to end the standoff over the strategic island. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen joined Trump at the United Nations General Assembly in New York for the trilateral signing ceremony.
The deal follows Trump’s repeated threats to annex Greenland—a move he insisted was a matter of “national security,” on account of the mineral-rich Arctic territory’s positioning between the U.S., Russia, and Europe. Trump has long argued that Denmark cannot be relied upon to protect the island. Tensions reached a critical point earlier this year, when he threatened to tariff European allies until Greenland fell under U.S. control, and suggested he may pull the U.S. out of NATO over the tussle.
The signed agreement notably stops short of Trump's call for the U.S. to take over Greenland as a U.S. territory.
Instead, in a speech at the U.N. gathering, Trump said the deal gives the U.S. "permanent control over security and all other needs on that territory" and emphasized that "no U.S. adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval."
Trump added that the new text “greatly protects” Europe and “very much enhances NATO."
Danish and Greenlandic officials have emphasized that the U.S. military arrangement will not compromise the territory’s sovereignty—a fear expressed by many Greenlanders following Trump’s pressure campaign.
Some critics have questioned whether the new deal differs much from the existing 1951 defense agreement that gave the U.S. military extensive rights in Greenland.
The U.S. already has one base in Greenland, the Pituffik Space Base, which is located in the northwest of the territory and provides missile warning and space surveillance capabilities. Per the new deal, the U.S. will be allowed to establish additional "defense area[s]" on the island, specifically at "Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig."
Upon the announcement of the deal on Friday, Trump had said the U.S. will "immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many" and specified that this is an "infinite life agreement, there is no end." A State Department official told TIME the deal ensures Greenland will forever be a part of the strategic defense area of North America.
Torrey Taussig, director of the transatlantic security initiative at the Atlantic Council, says the deal is a positive step for U.S. relations with its Western allies.
“This is a significant feat for Danish diplomacy in that they got this deal, in this form. They've taken the temperature down with this [Trump] Administration in a way that I don't see it really flaring up again, because the President is viewing it as a win," she tells TIME.
Here's what to know about the high-stakes agreement, what it means for Greenland’s sovereignty, and if it stands to end the standoff over the island.
What do we know about Trump's Greenland deal?
The deal marks a notable expansion of U.S. military infrastructure on the island, with plans for new "defense areas."
Trump has stressed that the agreement gives Washington “permanent control” over Greenland’s security, concerns over which he has positioned at the center of his campaign for the U.S. to control the island. “World peace is at stake,” he claimed, earlier this year, insisting that “China and Russia want Greenland, and there is not a thing that Denmark can do about it.”
Russia and China have eyed up emerging shipping routes in the Arctic and possibly new avenues to critical minerals.
The agreement, according to a State Department official, establishes “permanent” guarantees that “only the U.S. and our allies can make sensitive investments in Greenland, eliminating the previous status quo in which adversaries have been investing in Greenland's sensitive sectors without investment screening.”
The deal's permanence marks a shift from what was in place before, experts tell TIME.
“The old 1951 agreement was tied to the NATO treaty, and therefore contained the possibility that either NATO disappears, or Greenland or Denmark leave, and the agreement ends,” says Ole Wæver, a professor of international relations at the University of Copenhagen.
Meanwhile, the new agreement’s provisions regarding future investments in Greenland are noteworthy, but not groundbreaking, according to Taussig.
“On paper, it has advanced a few important security interests on behalf of the [Trump] Administration,” says Taussig of the terms. “But in substance, it's not like the Danes were looking to move out on significant Russian or Chinese military infrastructure projects in the near term.”
Some previous attempts at foreign investments in Greenland were reportedly thwarted by the U.S.
According to a 2019 report from the Wall Street Journal, the U.S. urged Denmark to finance airports in Greenland to counter a Chinese proposal for two airport projects, which was ultimately withdrawn.
What have Denmark and Greenland said?
Officials from Denmark and Greenland expressed their full backing of the new agreement at the signing ceremony.
“In the kingdom of Denmark, the United States has a friend that has always kept our word. An ally you have always been able to rely on.” Frederiksen said. “Seventy-five years ago, we entered into an agreement about the defense of Greenland; today we are signing a bigger and even better agreement. A deal that can last forever.”
In a statement to TIME, Frederiksen's office elaborated that the deal “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination" and "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area and is therefore also great for NATO and Europe.”
Nielsen said the new deal “takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods,” and “is about taking shared responsibility for a secure America, a secure Greenland, with mutual respect and a peaceful Arctic.”
Before travelling to New York, the Greenlandic leader acknowledged the fresh start and said he hopes there can now be more “peace around our country.”
The deal has also been welcomed by European leadership.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, shortly after the signing, celebrated the agreement for "strengthening security in the Arctic and North Atlantic."
Reflecting on her recent visit to Greenland, during which the E.U. extended a major investment boost in the territory, von der Leyen said her stay only underscored the "strategic importance of the region and the scale of the challenges."
While in Greenland, von der Leyen had commented on the “visible scars of climate change on the ice sheet,” and noted that a “new reality is taking shape” as the ice melts. “New trade routes, new security risks, new environmental concerns. Europe stands with Greenland. We will navigate these changes together,” she vowed.
How is NATO involved?
The agreement highlights NATO's significance, stipulating that "through enhanced presence, improved surveillance and increased cooperation and interoperability with NATO-Allies, the Kingdom of Denmark shall continue to address emerging threats and contribute to collective stability and security in the Arctic region."
Speaking at the signing, Nielsen insisted: "NATO matters. We believe that it is vital to keep NATO strong, also in the Arctic, where the alliance has a key role to play."
“The Arctic and the North Atlantic are essential for our collective security, and this agreement will help advance security, stability, and cooperation in this vital region,” NATO spokesperson Allison Hart told TIME.
No state that is not a member of NATO will be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland, per the agreement text, nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland, unless otherwise agreed by the parties.
“I do not see much changing for NATO with this deal,” says Taussig. “This is a good news story for the alliance—the fact that we now have a deal that takes away the political irritant [of annexation threats].”
NATO has bolstered its posture in the Arctic this year, with the launch of the Arctic Sentry in February, bringing military drills, surveillance, and presence in the region under one command.
In June, the alliance also established Forward Land Forces (FLF) Finland. Led by framework nation Sweden, "FLF Finland will enhance deterrence and the defence on NATO’s northeastern flank and contribute to the security of the Arctic and the High North," NATO said at the time of the launch.
Taussig says she expects this increased NATO presence in the Arctic to continue, not just because of this deal, "but because of the [Trump] Administration's rightful attention on Greenland, and also the reality of the security environment,” as Russia has ramped up operations in the region in recent years.
What did the 1951 agreement between the U.S. and Denmark give Washington?
Barring the permanence of the fresh agreement, and its tighter restrictions on investments from adversaries, Wæver says: “The reality is that the new deal is indeed very close to the 1951 treaty.”
The 1951 deal, titled the Defense of Greenland Agreement, was signed two years after both the U.S. and Denmark joined NATO as founding members. It provides the basis for Washington’s military operations and presence in the Arctic territory.
Per the agreement, the U.S. can establish and operate military bases on the island that Washington and Denmark both agree is “necessary for the development of the defense of Greenland and the rest of the North Atlantic Treaty area.”
The Pituffik Space Base, the last active American military installation in Greenland, has around 150 troops stationed there, according to the Wall Street Journal. Vice President J.D. Vance visited the base in March 2025, weeks after key elections in Greenland and amid heightened U.S. interest in the territory. He was met with signs of protest and opposition from residents of the territory.
Alongside general military operations, the 1951 arrangement also stipulated that the U.S. can station and house U.S. military and civilian personnel within said bases, control related aircraft and shipping, as well as develop necessary infrastructure. “The 1951 agreement already gave the United States relatively unfettered military access to Greenland,” says Taussig.
The 1951 agreement also confirmed Greenland’s and Denmark’s sovereignty over the island, and stated that military operations must follow local laws and regulations.
The terms of U.S. military presence were developed further in 2004 under the Igaliku agreement, in which Washington committed to consulting with and informing Greenland and Denmark of any significant changes to military facilities or operations within the territory.

articles.title: Zelensky, UK PM Burnham Meet in New York as Kyiv Warns Russia Preparing Massive Attack
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in New York on Tuesday, Sept. 22.
The talks, held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, focused on security, strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, preparations for winter and continued sanctions pressure on Moscow.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We now have intelligence that Russia is preparing a new massive attack against Ukraine,” Zelensky said following the meeting.
The Ukrainian leader thanked Britain for its continued support for the country’s energy sector, noting a new British contribution ahead of winter.
“We discussed in detail with Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Andy Burnham everything concerning security, the protection of our people, preparations for winter, and the available diplomatic opportunities,” Zelensky wrote.
The two leaders also discussed maintaining pressure on Moscow through sanctions.
“When Ukrainians live every day under the threat of missile and drone strikes, there can be no talk of lifting sanctions,” Zelensky said.
Kyiv and London share the position that sanctions should remain in place and be strengthened for as long as Russia’s war continues, he added.
The remarks came amid criticism in Kyiv over the removal of Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the EU sanctions list.
UK diplomatic push at the UN
The meeting formed part of Burnham’s broader diplomatic push at the UN General Assembly, where Ukraine has featured prominently in his discussions with international partners.
Trump Says Putin Is Willing to Meet as Diplomatic Momentum Continues
Earlier Tuesday, Burnham held his first face-to-face meeting with US President Donald Trump. The two spoke for around 40 minutes and discussed Ukraine alongside trade and other foreign policy issues.
Ahead of his trip, Burnham had signaled that he would use the UN gathering to push for increased support for Ukraine, including additional air defense capabilities and US-made Patriot systems.
The British government said Ukraine and support for the country through the coming winter would be among Burnham’s priorities during meetings with world leaders in New York.
London has also framed securing a “just and lasting peace” in Ukraine as one of Burnham’s priorities at this year’s UN General Assembly.

articles.title: EU removes two Russian billionaires from sanctions list
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — Two of Russia’s wealthiest men could soon be free to operate inside the EU after the bloc moved to lift restrictions on them and their empires as part of a high-stakes diplomatic play.
Capitals struck a deal on Tuesday to cut Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list, five diplomats told POLITICO, granted anonymity to speak frankly.
For more than a week, France had been holding up the EU’s entire framework of individual sanctions in an unexpected standoff, risking the expiry of the 3,000-odd listings if they weren’t renewed. Earlier talks ended without a deal Monday night after Baltic nations initially refused to sign off.
Advertisement
Paris launched a surprise campaign earlier this month calling for sanctions to be dropped on mining and telecoms billionaire Usmanov and citing a “national security” issue at play. Luxembourg, meanwhile, had long been asking for the delisting of banking magnate Fridman, who is suing the country for access to assets frozen by the Grand Duchy.
A number of countries — including Nordic and Baltic nations — had warned the move could jeopardize the entire sanctions list, leading others to lobby for their own narrow interests. The breakthrough came after Latvia, which had been the most vocal opponent, agreed to abstain on the plan.
As part of the deal, the current selection of names will be frozen for three years, effectively sidelining further debate until 2029. The agreement was due to take effect if capitals submitted their written consent by 6 p.m. on Tuesday.
“It is done,” said one of the diplomats. “The question is what Baltic countries got in return.”
Latvia defends deal
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs defended Riga’s climb-down, saying Latvia would “continue to advocate for the imposition of additional EU sanctions on Russia.” In a statement on the Latvian government website, the PM also noted that his had been “the only EU member state” to oppose the removal of “politically motivated individuals” from the individual sanctions list “until the very end.”
At the same time, he revealed, French President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks with Latvia on its accession to France’s nuclear deterrence initiative, and “also expressed his commitment to strengthening France’s military presence in Latvia, especially in the field of air defense.”
“Such a commitment will strengthen not only the security of Latvia but also of the entire NATO eastern flank,” he added.
Advertisement
EU capitals have struck a deal to remove Russia’s Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list.@benjaminhaddad called the outcome a win for European solidarity.
France had riled other EU members by announcing its support for Usmanov at short notice, saying only that it was related to “a specific national security issue” and that Paris “wishes to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr. Usmanov.”
Still, its European Affairs Minister Benjamin Haddad called Tuesday’s outcome a win for European solidarity.
“We keep a very strong united front on the sanctions on Russia,” Haddad told POLITICO. “We have these discussions. You have consideration of national security and others among member states. But the most important is that we’ve shown once again our unity and our resolve to put economic pressure on Russia for its war of aggression.”
Ukraine slams 'shameful' arrangement
Kyiv led criticism of the sanctions list maneuver, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha describing the delisting of Usmanov and Fridman as “shameful and unjustifiable.”
“Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he wrote on X.
The Financial Times reported that the delisting was part of a deal that could see French nationals released from detention in Azerbaijan. Paris has significantly stepped up its role in the South Caucasus in support of Armenia, a pro-EU democracy that has spent decades locked in conflict with Azerbaijan.
Advertisement
But some were concerned about the precedent that could set. “If the reports are confirmed, Europe must not turn sanctions into a bargaining chip,” said Latvian MEP Rihards Kols, a member of the Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee. “France has every right and duty to seek the release of its citizens. But the price cannot be relief for a Russian oligarch sanctioned for his links to the Putin regime.”
Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard also weighed in against the delistings. “I deeply regret the removal of two legally solid listings from the sanctions list,” she said. “Sanctions are a key element in the EU’s continued response to Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. We need to increase pressure on Russia and our support to Ukraine.”
Ukraine’s Sybiha noted that member countries could still individually push back against the transaction. “There is still a way to spoil the celebrations in Moscow,” he wrote. “I urge all EU member states to announce now that they will impose their own national sanctions on these two individuals [Usmanov and Fridman].”
The Latvian PM promised Latvia would do just that, and would “continue to use all legal instruments at its disposal to prevent the release of the funds and economic resources of these persons in Latvia.”
Info impasse
A handful of countries privately expressed frustration that further information had not been provided at Coreper, the meeting of ambassadors where sanctions rollover decisions are taken.
“Ambassadors were told that there are national security reasons. Coreper is not the right place to discuss those in detail,” said a senior French diplomat who was granted anonymity to speak frankly about the sensitive discussions last week. “Member states were told a week ago that if they needed more precision, they could get it through the appropriate channels.”
Usmanov has consistently denied supporting Russia’s war effort, rejected the idea he is an oligarch, and campaigned for his removal from the sanctions list. Fridman has likewise argued the seizure of his assets is unlawful.
“Maybe those two oligarchs are very happy today,” Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told a press conference at the U.N. in New York on Tuesday. “But they don’t know me. I will come to Europe with the same names again.”

articles.title: Trump says talks in NYC with Zelensky will cover Russia–Ukraine negotiations and Patriot interceptor production in Ukraine
articles.body:
Trump says talks in NYC with Zelensky will cover Russia–Ukraine negotiations and Patriot interceptor production in Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and U.S. President Donald Trump have begun their meeting on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. Before their closed-door talks, they spoke to the press.
Answering reporters’ questions, Trump said he would discuss the status of negotiations with Russia, the production of Patriot interceptor missiles in Ukraine, and Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he again said are driving up global diesel prices.
Zelensky expressed hope that the war with Russia could end before winter, though until recently he had doubted that was possible. Trump did not rule out another meeting with Vladimir Putin in an effort to secure a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine.
Update: Zelensky and Trump’s closed-door talks lasted 40 minutes. Afterward, the Ukrainian president spoke to reporters again. He said Kyiv is ready for a complete ceasefire with Moscow on attacks against energy infrastructure, but that it must be reciprocal. “If we don’t attack each other’s energy facilities, then [we don’t attack] any energy facilities. That’s our proposal,” Zelensky said. He added that the U.S. will convey this position to Russia.
After Trump was reelected to a second term, the U.S. began mediating negotiations between Russia and Ukraine. The talks were suspended in early 2026 as the U.S. entered the war with Iran. In August, however, the U.S. resumed its mediation efforts. CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Trump’s special envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, visited Moscow and later met with Zelensky.
Among other issues, the two sides discussed a mutual halt to attacks on energy facilities. Trump even announced that Russia and Ukraine had reached an energy truce, but it quickly became clear that he had spoken too soon. The latest round of U.S.-mediated talks has so far produced no results, but both Ukraine and Russia have said they are willing to continue talks.

articles.title: Trump signs ‘fantastic’ Greenland security deal with Denmark
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump signs a trilateral security agreement between the United States, Denmark and Greenland, in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images
U.S. President Donald Trump has signed a deal on the future of Greenland, ending months of transatlantic tensions over his demand to take over the North Atlantic territory.
Trump told the United Nations General Assembly in New York that the agreement gives the U.S. “permanent control over security and all other needs.” He said: “We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe and other places.”
No U.S. adversary will be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland or make sensitive investments without American written approval, he said.
Advertisement
Trump promised to build two “very major military bases” on the territory, adding that he’s “formed a bond” with the people of “beautiful” Denmark and the Greenlanders during the negotiations.
According to the agreement released by the Danish government, the two new American bases will be located in Narsarsuaq, in southern Greenland at the site of the former American Bluie West One base which closed in the 1950s. The other will be located in Mestersvig, eastern Greenland, currently home to Denmark's Sirius Dog Sled Patrol unit, which will be refurbished.
The U.S. military will also have “free access” to air, land and sea routes on the island between the two bases. Greenland is already home to the U.S. Pituffik Space Base, where about 150 American troops are stationed to operate a ballistic missile monitoring site to protect North America from long-range missile attack.
“I know it’s going to be a long-term, fantastic relationship,” Trump said at the signing ceremony later, alongside the prime ministers of Denmark, Mette Frederiksen, and Greenland, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
Frederiksen thanked Trump for the deal, labeling it a good one for the U.S., Denmark, and Greenland that would keep enemies and adversaries at bay.
The agreement amends and builds on the previous 1951 agreement between the governments of Denmark and the U.S., which gave the U.S. wide latitude to build new military installations and move about the island. It does not cancel or entirely replace the 1951 deal.
Advertisement
New elements make some pointed revisions, however, stipulating that no non-NATO nation can open a base on the island or mine for critical minerals or rare earths without the agreement of the three signatories.
Trump has often spoken about Chinese and Russian military activities around Greenland, claiming earlier this year that, "if you take a look outside of Greenland right now, there are Russian destroyers. There are Chinese destroyers … there are Russian submarines all over the place. We're not going to have Russia or China occupy Greenland, and that's what they're going to do if we don't."
NATO officials have quietly pushed back against those claims, with one diplomat saying “we’re not seeing any Chinese activity” around Greenland, while Russian movements in the High North haven’t changed significantly and there’s little, if any, Russian presence near Greenland.
In a nod to the new prevalence of aerial and naval drones, the agreement also gives the power to Denmark and Greenland to control where — and if — new bases for unmanned platforms can be built on the island. “Denmark together with Greenland shall review requests to establish unmanned military installations in Greenland outside of the Defense Areas under accelerated governmental approval procedures,” the agreement states.
“Seventy-five years ago, we entered into an agreement about the defense of Greenland,” Frederiksen said. “Today we are signing an even bigger and better agreement — a deal that can last forever.”
Nielsen, Greenland’s premier, said the territory had been supporting U.S. security since World War II. “We are, have been and will remain a steadfast friend of the United States and a part of the Western alliance. Your security is our security, and our security is your security,” he said.
Advertisement
At the start of the year, Trump horrified European allies with his push to annex the sovereign Danish territory and threatened to destabilize NATO, given that Denmark has been a member since the alliance was founded in 1949.
In the end, the text of the agreement that Trump signed explicitly reaffirmed Danish sovereignty and the right of Greenlanders to self-determination.
Denmark’s European allies welcomed the resolution. European Council President António Costa congratulated Frederiksen and Nielsen but did not mention Trump by name.
The deal is “a positive step for transatlantic cooperation and Arctic security, grounded in respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,” Costa said. “The EU stands ready to continue working closely with Greenland, Denmark and our transatlantic partners for a peaceful, secure and prosperous Arctic.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also welcomed the deal. “It is good news that the negotiations of recent months have led to a mutually acceptable solution in line with international law,” he said.

articles.title: UNGA 2026: What to know as world leaders gather in New York
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UNGA 2026: What to know as world leaders gather in New York
Almost 130 heads of state and government are gathering in New York this week as the high-level general debate of the UN General Assembly gets underway.
The general debate is the centrepiece of the UNGA's annual High-level Week, giving world leaders a platform to set out their positions and priorities on major international issues.
The 81st session of the General Assembly formally opened on 8 September, with Bangladesh's Khalilur Rahman taking over as its president.
When is the general debate taking place?
The general debate opens at 0900 local time (1300 GMT) on Tuesday 22 September and runs through to Saturday 26 September. It will resume for a final day on Monday 28 September, with no session held on Sunday.
The debate is divided into two daily sessions, with the morning session running from 0900 to 1445 (1300 to 1845 GMT) and the afternoon session from 1500 to 2100 (1900 to 0100 GMT the following day).
Speakers are asked to observe a voluntary 15-minute limit, although statements frequently run longer and sessions continue until all scheduled speakers have delivered their addresses.
Who is speaking and when?
Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will open proceedings on Tuesday by presenting his annual report and is expected to deliver his final address to the general debate before leaving office at the end of the year.
He will be followed by General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman, who will formally open the debate.
The first two countries to speak will follow a long-running UN tradition. Brazil has opened the country statements since 1955, while the United States, as the host country, traditionally speaks second.
US President Donald Trump is expected to take the podium after Brazil on Tuesday morning.
Jordan's King Abdullah II, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani are also due to address the assembly during Tuesday's morning session.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa will open Wednesday's morning session, followed shortly afterwards by Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Mohammed al-Menfi, chairman of Libya's Presidential Council, is also due to speak during the morning session.
The State of Palestine, the Holy See and the European Union are also invited to participate despite not being UN member states.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas is expected to address the assembly by prerecorded video after the United States denied visas to Palestinian officials. UN member states voted to allow his remote participation.
What is on the agenda?
The 81st General Assembly is being held under the theme "Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all".
Alongside the general debate, High-level Week features a series of meetings on some of the major challenges facing the international community.
These include high-level events on climate action and a just transition and the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development on 23 September, sea-level rise on 24 September, pandemic prevention, preparedness and response on 25 September, and the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration against racism on 28 September.
A high-level meeting on the total elimination of nuclear weapons will follow on 29 September.
Many leaders' speeches are also expected to focus on the wars and conflicts across the Middle East and Ukraine, the global economy, artificial intelligence and the UN's growing funding pressures.
The week comes against a backdrop of mounting geopolitical divisions and growing pressure on the multilateral system, with the UN also facing questions over how to make the organisation more efficient and effective.
Who will replace Guterres as UN chief?
The race to succeed Guterres as the UN's next secretary-general is not expected to conclude this week.
While the General Assembly formally appoints the secretary-general, the 15-member Security Council must first agree on and recommend a candidate.
Seven candidates remain in the running, including former Senegalese president Macky Sall, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi and UN trade agency chief Rebeca Grynspan.
The other declared candidates are Guyana's UN ambassador and former foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Ecuadorian diplomat and former minister Ivonne Baki, former General Assembly president Maria Fernanda Espinosa of Ecuador and former Ugandan foreign minister and UN undersecretary-general Olara Otunnu.
Former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet withdrew from the race on Saturday.
Several Security Council members have said they want a woman to become UN secretary-general for the first time. Since the organisation was founded in 1945, all nine people to hold the post have been men.
Guterres's second and final term will end on 31 December.

articles.title: Pentagon: laser defense needs hardware, not more demos
articles.body:
- Assistant Secretary of War Michael Dodd said Sept. 22 that high-energy laser programs must move from demonstrations to ruggedized, fielded systems for air and missile defense.
- The U.S. Army has already committed to a Joint Laser Weapon System program and a $464.8 million laser contract with AeroVironment, while the Navy and Air Force have not.
Assistant Secretary of War for Critical Technologies Michael Dodd said the Department of War needs to move directed energy weapons out of testing and into the field, arguing in a Sept. 22 post on X that high-energy laser programs have proven the technology works and now need ruggedized, deployable systems for air and missile defense.
Dodd did not announce a new program or contract in the post. His comments add to a public campaign he has run for months, pushing the military services to commit money and timelines to fielding lasers and high-power microwave weapons rather than running further demonstrations.
The Army has already made that commitment. It awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million contract this year for the Enduring-High Energy Laser program, a 30-kilowatt system the company has called the first production contract for a directed energy weapon in U.S. history. The Army has also agreed to transition its Joint Laser Weapon System into a formal program of record. Dodd has said his office funds prototypes and early, small-scale deployments, but expects the individual services to buy directed energy systems by the dozens or hundreds once a design proves itself.
The Navy and Air Force have not made comparable commitments. Dodd said in August he is pressing both services to follow the Army’s lead, with the Navy interested in much higher-powered systems, in the hundreds of kilowatts to a megawatt range, to defend ships against cruise missiles, a heavier requirement than the counter-drone systems the Army is pursuing.
Cost is central to the Pentagon’s argument for lasers. Officials have said a single laser shot can cost around $3.50, compared to millions of dollars for a Patriot interceptor missile, against drones that can cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece. Dodd has pointed to that mismatch as the reason directed energy needs to scale quickly, saying in March that the department aims to field directed energy weapons broadly within 36 months.
The technology still faces real constraints. Laser and microwave systems draw on rare earth elements and other critical minerals largely processed in China, and Dodd has acknowledged that per-system costs remain high because production has not scaled up. He has also pushed industry to shrink the size, weight and power demands of these weapons so they can fly on aircraft, telling contractors in August to bring “hardware we can put on a range and stress” rather than further concept presentations.
The Air Force has tested high-power microwave systems for counter-drone use, including the trailer-mounted THOR system, though its most recent publicly disclosed test dates to 2023. The Air Force Research Laboratory has said it is developing a follow-on system.

articles.title: Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran in UN speech (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran in UN speech (VIDEO)
President Donald Trump has threatened to “annihilate” Iran if negotiations fail, saying he faces a “big decision” as he predicted no deal with Tehran would come until after the US midterm elections in November.
Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump defended the US-Israeli war with Iran and accused Tehran of deliberately delaying an agreement.
“But I have a big decision to make. Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” Trump asked, before presenting the alternative: “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly?”
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he continued.
Trump nevertheless said he believed an agreement would be reached “right after the election.” Later in the speech, he said Washington and Tehran would “definitely get it done… one way or the other.”
Trump also called on other countries to join the US in enforcing the “complete economic isolation” of Iran until Tehran meets Washington’s conditions.
Members of the Iranian delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall, leaving only one lower-level delegate seated, as Trump defended the nearly seven-month conflict, accusing Tehran of seeking nuclear weapons, supporting terrorism and attacking commercial shipping.
Hours later, however, Trump struck a more conciliatory tone, revealing that his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had held a “very productive meeting” with Iranian representatives. Witkoff said mediators shuttled between the US and Iranian delegations throughout the day and completed a round of discussions that Washington hoped would prove “constructive and promising.”
Iranian state media confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met US negotiators on the sidelines of the General Assembly at Washington’s request. According to the report, Tehran used the meeting to present its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including an end to the US naval blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Iran’s military, meanwhile, responded defiantly to Trump’s remarks, warning that further US or Israeli escalation would be met with stronger retaliatory strikes.

articles.title: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran in bombastic UN speech
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran in bombastic UN speech
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he has to decide whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate" the country, in a bombastic speech to the United Nations that appeared tailored to war-weary American voters.
The 80-year-old president's threat came amid repeated boasts that under him the United States is successfully confronting its adversaries and reshaping the world order to its own advantage.
"While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them," Trump told the room full of world leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York.
Despite claiming credit as a peacemaker, Trump delivered a jarring warning as he sought to justify the nearly seven-month war against Iran, which he said was launched to stop Tehran acquiring nuclear weapons.
"I have a big decision to make -- will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country?" Trump said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival?"
Trump reiterated that he believed Iran would "make a deal right after" the US midterm elections in November, in which his Republican party faces losing control of Congress, at least partly due to high fuel prices caused by the unpopular war.
'Military might'
Much of the rest of his speech was dedicated to proclaiming his own achievements in making the United States the "most powerful country in the world."
Trump threatened to use the "unmatched military might" of the US to secure Washington's interests in Latin America, and said the island of Cuba would soon "fall".
He also hailed a deal with Greenland under which he said Washington would build two bases in the Arctic territory. Trump was signing the deal with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland on the sidelines of the UN.
The Greenland deal has sparked bitter divisions within long-term US alliances including NATO and revived fears that under Trump, Washington is no longer a reliable partner.
The volatile US president also renewed his attack on what he said were "globalist" bodies, including the United Nations itself and the International Criminal Court, which he urged other countries to boycott.
Trump's 37-minute speech to the world body was perhaps less fiery than last year's, which was characterized by Trump's extraordinary accusations of UN sabotage.
Those claims were sparked when an escalator in New York briefly stopped working and the teleprompter glitched. This year Trump ascended the escalator with wife Melania without a hitch, and appeared to read his speech faithfully from the teleprompter.
Guterres warnings
Trump has regularly attacked the UN and its outgoing leader Antonio Guterres since returning to office.
Guterres kicked off the week of speeches by warning of the "specter of ethnic cleansing" in Israel's settlements expansion in the occupied West Bank.
He also called for US-Chinese dialogue on the future of AI and singled out global energy companies for treating the atmosphere "as an open sewer."
As well as his closely watched speech to the General Assembly, Trump was holding side meetings with Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Japanese premier Sanae Takaichi.
Trump was also set to hold his first meeting with Venezuela's interim leader Delcy Rodriguez. Rodriguez has governed under intense American pressure since US forces captured her predecessor Nicolas Maduro in January.

Lithuania’s parliament votes to remove ban on hosting nuclear weapons in first of three votes

articles.title: Iran ready to reopen Hormuz within 7 days if US eases pressure
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran ready to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days if US eases military pressure and lifts blockade
Iran can reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday.
On Sunday, Iran's military central command said it was informed the US was preparing to restart military operations with the support of regional countries, and warned this would lead to Tehran's retaliation "without limitations and considerations".
"The US needs to announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official, and then agree on a timeline for how the process will move forward", the senior Iranian official said, adding the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly is in New York and has full authority to revive diplomacy with the United States.
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who left Tehran for New York on Tuesday morning, will not meet US President Donald Trump at the UN headquarters in New York, the official told Reuters.
The Iranian official said details on an agreement to end hostilities with Washington can be discussed in New York via mediators, explaining that Tehran's proposal was delivered to the US via mediators on 16 September.
"The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy", the official said, adding that Tehran would welcome a revival of diplomacy if Washington takes tangible steps.
Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday the US is open to speaking with Iranians at the UN General Assembly, but no meeting is currently scheduled.
"We're open to that. I don't think anything is scheduled at this point, but we're certainly open to something like that, especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about," Rubio said in an interview with NBC's "Today" show.
"And that is the fact that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. They just simply can't," he insisted.
Both the United States and Israel—who jointly launched a war on Iran at the end of February—possess nuclear weapons.

articles.title: Lithuania’s Seimas backs move to remove constitutional ban on nuclear weapons
articles.body:
Lithuania’s parliament on Tuesday backed a proposal to remove from the constitution a ban on stationing weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on the country’s territory, opening the way for a potential future deployment of NATO nuclear weapons.
The proposal received 99 votes in favour, 13 against and five abstentions during its consideration in the Seimas. The vote advances the constitutional amendment but does not itself authorise the deployment of nuclear weapons in Lithuania.
The Constitution’s Article 137 currently states that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said the first vote on adopting the constitutional amendment is scheduled for October 6, with the final vote planned for January 12, 2027.
Constitutional amendments require two votes separated by at least three months, with at least 94 of the 141 lawmakers required to approve the measure at each final stage.
Remigijus Žemaitaitis, leader of the Nemunas Dawn party, opposed the proposal, arguing that Russia and Belarus could use it for propaganda purposes. He also said nuclear-armed states would be able to use nuclear weapons to defend Lithuania if necessary without removing the constitutional provision.
He argued that the relevant constitutional article should only be changed through a referendum.
Ignas Vėgėlė, a member of the parliament’s mixed group, questioned why the proposal would remove the entire provision rather than only the restriction on weapons of mass destruction. The article also prohibits foreign military bases.
“Why are we deleting this part of the sentence as well? Are we planning to hand over Lithuanian territory to military bases that we will not control or manage?” Vėgėlė asked.
He noted that Lithuania’s Constitutional Court has ruled that allied foreign military bases can operate in Lithuania if they are established by allies and remain under Lithuanian control. He argued that a similar principle should apply to weapons of mass destruction.
Laurynas Kasčiūnas, parliamentary leader of the opposition Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats, said nuclear weapons are a key component of deterrence.
He said nuclear deterrence helped prevent the Cold War from becoming a direct military conflict and argued that Lithuania should not maintain restrictions that do not apply to some of its NATO allies.
“We are the only country in the region that has this restriction. Latvia does not have it, Estonia does not have it, Poland does not have it, Finland has just removed it,” Kasčiūnas said.
He cited a hypothetical scenario in which a US allied ship carrying nuclear weapons or a nuclear-capable aircraft might need to pass through Lithuanian territory for deterrence purposes.
Kasčiūnas stressed that removing the ban would not mean Lithuania had decided to station nuclear weapons there, but said eliminating the constitutional restriction would give the country more options as part of NATO’s deterrence arrangements.
Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee and a Social Democrat, also said Lithuania should not create obstacles to NATO’s nuclear deterrence or become the weaker link in the alliance’s regional security posture.
“Lithuania must clearly show our allies and adversaries that we will defend our independence by all means,” Motuzas said. “We cannot be less protected than other NATO countries.”
He said changing the constitution would send a strong signal intended to reduce the risk of military aggression.
Liberal Movement leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen said deterrence should not be viewed as an escalation of war.
“Today’s vote is about ensuring that we are not weaker,” she said.
The proposal comes amid broader discussions in Europe about nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron has promoted the idea of developing a European nuclear deterrence framework under which partner countries could potentially host French strategic aircraft equipped with nuclear weapons.
The Financial Times reported in June that the United States was considering deploying nuclear weapons in additional NATO countries in Europe, although no such deployment in Lithuania has been announced.
