articles.title: Russia demands a "strong peace" from Ukraine, but on its own terms — Peskov
articles.body:
Russia demands a "strong peace" from Ukraine, but on its own terms — Peskov
Kyiv • UNN
Putin's spokesman said that the Kremlin opposes a ceasefire and demands territorial concessions from Ukraine, its renunciation of NATO, and demilitarization.
Russia advocates for a "solid peace, peace forever, rather than a ceasefire that, essentially, will achieve nothing." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said this in a comment to Russian "media," reports UNN.
Details
According to the Russian dictator's spokesman, "the situation in Ukraine is deteriorating every day, and this will continue."

Russia demands that Ukraine fully withdraw its troops from the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia regions, as well as officially renounce any plans to integrate into NATO.

articles.title: Danish defense startup guarding undersea cables runs on 15 Ukrainian suppliers. Ukrainian fund is putting in €2 million in it
articles.body:
A Ukrainian fund is investing in a Danish defense startup, a reversal for a country far better known for taking in foreign capital than for sending it abroad. Resist.UA is backing BlueShadow, a maritime security firm run by a former US Navy submarine commander but largely engineered in Ukraine, to build defenses for coasts and undersea cables against drones and hybrid attacks.
BlueShadow is registered in Denmark, but almost its entire engineering team works in Ukraine, and it folds gear from more than 15 Ukrainian suppliers of drones, sensors, and communications into a single system.
Resist.UA, which signed a letter of intent to join the company's €2 million pre-seed round, runs a new €50 million fund, Resist 2.0, designed to bring Ukraine's battlefield-proven technology to global markets.
Ukraine engineers the Danish startup
The company was founded in 2025 and is led by Charles Maher, a former commander of a US Navy nuclear submarine, according to Defender Media.
This summer, it registered as a Ukrainian legal entity and builds on Ukrainian components, planning to fit its maritime platforms with M-Fly's RB-220 gimbal, a day-and-night targeting sensor used until now only on flying drones.
The two sides first met in January 2026 and formalized the partnership as BlueShadow raised its round and Resist.UA launched its second fund.
The systems guard the sea
BlueShadow is building two of them. BlueDragon, still in development, is designed to shield Ukraine's coastal cities, ports, and shipping lanes from drone strikes. BlueSentry, which the company plans to launch in October, is aimed at protecting ports, offshore wind farms, undersea cables, and maritime borders from hybrid attack, the kind of sabotage that has repeatedly damaged Baltic Sea infrastructure.
"This partnership will fuel the next phase of our mission to protect people, infrastructure, commerce, and natural resources at sea," the company said.
Ukraine's defense tech turns outward
Ukrainian defense technology, tested in real combat, has drawn growing investor interest, and Ukrainian figures are now building funds to channel it: the former Defense Minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, is raising what he calls the country's largest defense-tech venture fund.

articles.title: Can all Russians be held responsible for the war in Ukraine? A heated online debate runs up against international law’s principle of individual responsibility.
articles.body:
Can all Russians be held responsible for the war in Ukraine? A heated online debate runs up against international law’s principle of individual responsibility.
What happened?
An episode of “The Breakfast Show” featuring sociologist Konstantin Gaaze has prompted fierce debate on social media — particularly over his claim that Russians bear collective responsibility for Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Here is the exact quote:
Living in the territory of an aggressor state violates international law. Citizenship in an aggressor country makes you an international criminal.
What does international law say about this?
International humanitarian law does not support that claim.
The most comprehensive international instrument governing these issues is the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC). It says civilians bear no criminal or other responsibility for a war started or waged by their state.
The key principle is individual culpability, which rules out collective punishment, particularly for civilians. Citizens who were not personally involved in planning the aggression and did not commit crimes cannot be prosecuted.
Here is what the relevant articles say:
- Article 8 bis. Responsibility for the “crime of aggression” — the ICC’s official term — applies only to a narrow group of people: those “in a position effectively to exercise control over or to direct the political or military action of a State.” In other words, no one can be prosecuted under this article merely for being a citizen. Prosecutors must prove that the person held power at the highest levels of government and made key decisions.
- Article 25. This article further establishes that only individuals can be held criminally responsible. A person can be held responsible for a crime within the ICC’s jurisdiction if they committed it alone or with someone else, ordered or incited it, or intentionally helped carry it out.
The catch, however, is that the ICC cannot try Russians — even those directly involved in starting the war — specifically for the “crime of aggression.” Russia has not ratified the Rome Statute or its amendments, and Article 15 bis expressly prohibits prosecuting nationals of states that have not signed the treaty for this crime.
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well. It’s always for the same reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me whenever it works for them. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their place. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
What about the arrest warrant for Putin?
The ICC arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova are unrelated to the “crime of aggression.”
Both are accused of war crimes, which fall under a different provision of the Rome Statute, Article 8. In this case, it does not matter whether Russia ratified the statute because the crimes were committed in Ukraine, which has accepted the ICC’s jurisdiction.
But wasn’t the “crime of aggression” also committed in Ukraine?
The situation is more complicated when it comes to the “crime of aggression” because countries could not agree on how to handle it. When Article 8 bis was later added, it created two ways to hold a country’s leaders responsible for the “crime of aggression”:
- First, when a country ratifies the Rome Statute, its leaders accept an obligation not to commit the crime of aggression.
- Second, a special U.N. Security Council resolution can make the nationality of an aggressor state’s leaders irrelevant. But this route is blocked in Russia’s case because Russia is a permanent member of the Security Council and would inevitably veto such a resolution.
The ICC decisions ordering the arrests of Putin and Lvova-Belova list specific war crimes:
- “Unlawful deportation or transfer or unlawful confinement”
- “The transfer, directly or indirectly, by the Occupying Power of parts of its own civilian population into the territory it occupies, or the deportation or transfer of all or parts of the population of the occupied territory within or outside this territory”
That explains the case against Putin. But can any other Russians be tried by the ICC?
Yes — quite a few.
These legal provisions are difficult to parse. Put as simply as possible, the picture is this: The ICC cannot try any Russian for the “crime of aggression,” much less all Russians at once.
But the ICC can prosecute Russian citizens for other categories of crimes, including war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide. This applies not only to those who made key political decisions but also to lower-level perpetrators.

This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Ukraine shoots down Russian drones by hundred thousand: 350,000 this year, filmed and verified hit by hit in DELTA
articles.body:
Ukraine's forces have shot down more than 350,000 Russian drones since the start of the year. The count, some 220,000 fixed-wing drones, 100,000 quadcopters, and 31,000 long-range Gerans, was filmed hit by hit in the DELTA combat system and verified by the Brave1 defense-innovation cluster, the Defense Ministry said.
Meanwhile, Russia is now threatening NATO countries directly, its drones probing Polish and Baltic skies, and those countries manage to down only a small fraction of what crosses their borders. In one incursion, Poland shot down just four of about 19 Russian drones.
Ukraine's 350,000 is the record of a force that has had to master drone defense at an industrial scale, night after night.
The tally runs to hundreds of thousands
Most of the kills belong to the Defense Forces' unmanned-systems units, which downed more than 320,000 Russian fixed-wing and copter drones. Those units, together with mobile fire groups and army aviation, also brought down faster Geran-type attack drones.
The pace has been relentless: in August alone, Ukraine destroyed some 35,000 fixed-wing drones and nearly 24,000 copters, the ministry said.
DELTA verifies every hit
Every downing is logged and confirmed in DELTA, the digital system Ukraine uses to run the battlefield, and which the ministry calls a key to its edge over Russia. Filming and verifying each kill lets commanders study how it was done and scale up whatever works.
The purpose is concrete: knocking down fixed-wing drones blinds Russian reconnaissance, and blunts strikes on cities and critical infrastructure, while downing copters keeps Russia from finding and hitting front-line positions. Each drone stopped, the ministry says, is potentially the life of a Ukrainian soldier or civilian saved.
The same threat now shadows NATO
That threat is spreading. Prime Minister Donald Tusk told Poland's parliament that intelligence points to Russian plans for drone and missile strikes on countries backing Ukraine.
The allies being warned are the ones that have struggled to stop even a handful of drones, while Ukraine, out of necessity, has learned to bring them down by the hundred thousand.

The EU locked in its sanctions on Russia for an unprecedented three years this week, and paid for it by letting two of the country's richest men off the list. Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman were delisted at the insistence of Slovakia, France, and Luxembourg, DW reported.

At the same time, he stated that he "is grateful to Ursula for her willingness to work on adding more Russian individuals to the EU sanctions lists."
The step was a bargain of durability for names. articles.title: Iraq extends armed groups disarmament deadline to June 2027
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraq extends armed groups disarmament deadline to June 2027
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi has agreed with leaders of the country's powerful pro-Iran political bloc to give armed groups until June 2027 to complete their disarmament, sources in Baghdad told The New Arab, extending a process initially expected to conclude by the end of September.
The agreement was reached with leaders of Iraq's pro-Iran Coordination Framework, which holds the largest bloc in parliament, before Al-Zaidi travelled to the United States for the UN General Assembly and talks with US officials, the sources said.
The move effectively gives powerful armed factions another nine months to bring their weapons under state control, amid continued resistance from some groups and disagreements over how the process should be implemented.
Al-Zaidi had previously committed to bringing weapons outside state control under government authority by 30 September, following attacks by pro-Iran armed groups on US bases during the war on Iran and subsequent US air strikes on their positions.
Under the new plan, the process would instead be completed by 30 June 2027, with the implementation phase expected to begin in January.
By extending the timeframe, Al-Zaidi hopes to remove the remaining justifications cited by armed factions that have refused to surrender their weapons or fully integrate into Iraq's state security forces.
A new directorate will reportedly be established within the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) to oversee the process, operating under the supervision of the Iraqi government.
The body would be responsible for receiving and cataloguing weapons, ammunition and military equipment held by armed groups, identifying where they are stored and establishing procedures governing their use.
However, the weapons would remain within facilities overseen by the PMF rather than being handed directly to the Iraqi government, a provision that could become a key point of contention with Washington.
Members and leaders of armed factions would also receive immunity from prosecution and retain the right to participate in Iraq's political process if they sign pledges to refrain from armed activity outside state authority.
Disagreement over who controls the weapons
A key dispute remains over who will ultimately control the groups' arsenals.
Washington has pushed for the Iraqi state to establish a monopoly over weapons, while the proposed arrangement would leave the PMF playing a central role in overseeing arms surrendered by the factions.
The US reportedly considers transferring weapons from faction-controlled warehouses to storage facilities that remain under PMF authority insufficient to meet its demands for weapons to be brought fully under state control.
Baghdad, however, faces considerable obstacles in forcing the issue.
Several powerful armed groups continue to resist full disarmament, while the Iraqi government has sought to avoid a military confrontation with factions that retain significant military and political influence.
Pro-Iran groups have also set a series of conditions for giving up their weapons, including the full withdrawal of US forces from Iraq and Turkish troops from northern Iraq, the restoration of what they describe as Iraq's full sovereignty over its territory, stronger Iraqi air defences and federal control over the borders of the autonomous Kurdistan region.
The dispute has complicated Al-Zaidi's attempt to fulfil his pledge to bring all weapons under state authority while avoiding a confrontation with groups that form part of the country's broader political and security establishment.
'Very difficult, indeed impossible'
Uday al-Khadran, a member of the Coordination Framework, told The New Arab that resolving the issue by the end of September had become "very difficult, indeed impossible", citing resistance among armed groups and the absence of mechanisms capable of implementing the process.
He nevertheless said the factions would eventually comply with the government's demands.
"Everyone will ultimately hand over the weapons," al-Khadran said. "But the matter requires arrangements, understandings and sufficient time to complete the process."
He added that negotiations were continuing and that the parties had yet to reach a final agreement on all aspects of the plan.
The priority, al-Khadran said, was to reach an arrangement acceptable to the parties involved that would ultimately bring weapons under state control.

articles.title: Witkoff, Kushner meet mediators as Iran sets demands for reopening Hormuz

US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with mediators to discuss a possible deal to end the Iran conflict.
Trump told reporters at the United Nations that US officials had had a "very good" three-hour meeting on Tuesday with the Iranian delegation.
He said that Washington and Tehran were moving toward a settlement, while a senior Iranian official said Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the US eased military pressure and lifted its blockade on Iranian ports.
"We are completely isolating Iran financially and simply applying pressure, because we hope they will do the right thing quickly-before it’s too late," Trump said. "You know, there will come a point when it’s too late, and we will no longer have the option of allowing them to survive as a nation."
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in a meeting during which Iran's conditions to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz were conveyed to the US, according to Iran's state media.
Iran sets Hormuz reopening conditions amid renewed US talks
Conditions for reopening the strait include immediate lifting of the naval blockade, immediate release of frozen Iranian assets and end of war across all 'resistance' fronts, state media added.
Trump's remarks came just hours after he repeated a threat at the UN General Assembly to annihilate Iran if it failed to strike a deal.
Speaking after a meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations in New York, Trump said: "They want to talk to us. They have been talking to us; even today they've been talking to us, and the relationship is developing.
"But we can't let them - and they understand that - we can't let them have a nuclear weapon."

US President Donald Trump also met with Middle Eastern leaders on the sidelines of the UN to discuss bringing an end to the war in Gaza and addressing tensions with Iran.
During the meeting, Trump commended the US and its partners' efforts in the region and praised the participating nations for their regional cooperation, crediting them with successfully delivering humanitarian aid to Gaza and securing the release of hostages held there.
Trump said the nations represented at the meeting "invested billions of dollars in helping Gaza - in helping the people."
"The people around this table made that possible," he added.
Referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Trump stated that he's a "tough cookie, don't mess around with him, he's tough, he's a fantastic guy."

articles.title: Lithuania plans key substation near Russia, fortified against explosive drones
articles.body:
Lithuania plans key substation near Russia, fortified against explosive drones
VILNIUS/WARSAW, Sept 22 - Lithuania is planning defences against military drones at a key future power grid substation linking the Baltic states with western Europe in an area that intelligence sources say Russia could target with a false flag attack.
The construction plans include fencing strong enough to resist an explosives-laden truck, sensors searching for possible tunnels dug by hostile actors, and concrete "sarcophagi" for transformers to withstand any drone attack, Litgrid CEO Andrius Semeskevicius told Reuters.
"Previously, when designing our grid, we planned for natural disasters. Now, we think about all possible hybrid and non-hybrid threats", he said in an interview.
The Gizai substation, to be built some 30 km (19 miles) west of the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, will be the first new installation in the region since Russia launched its full-blown invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It will be part of a key grid section being built to ensure steady power supply to the Baltic states in case of a wider conflict.
Its route through a section of Poland and Lithuania squeezed between Russia and its ally Belarus -- the so-called Suwalki Gap -- has long caused security concerns within the NATO military alliance, of which Warsaw and Vilnius are both members.
Such concerns increased this month after a series of sabotage attacks against Germany's electricity grid that Berlin blamed on Moscow. Russia denied any involvement.
Intelligence sources told Reuters last month the region is worried about a false flag drone attack by Russia to test NATO unity. A false flag attack is an operation designed to deceive people about who is actually responsible for carrying it out.
NO ORDINARY CONCRETE
The Gizai substation will be the crucial node of the interconnection with Poland called Harmony Link, which completes the connection of the Baltic grids with the rest of the European Union after they decoupled from Russia's grid last year.
"For Lithuania, this line is absolutely crucial, it's their lifeline if the system collapses," an official from a grid company in the region told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity. "The timing of this decision is linked to increasing tensions in the region and rising threats of sabotage."
The substation will be spread across a 35-hectare site, so a single hit from a military drone would only harm a limited amount of equipment, Semeskevicius said.
The distance of buildings from the fence means protection "in case someone throws a Molotov cocktail inside", he added.
"We are designing Gizai for a new reality... we are protecting ourselves from multiple Shahed drones, which could crash-land with 100 kilograms of explosives", he said.
Russia uses low-cost, long-range Shahed attack drones, designed by Iran, to wreak havoc on Ukrainian military infrastructure, cities and energy facilities, depriving millions of people of heating and lighting.
"We cannot use simple concrete, it needs to be custom-made, for stronger resistance", said Semeskevicius. The right concrete has threads of plastic to reinforce it and prevent it from crumbling, he said.
The substation includes several duplicate units of key equipment, for example, so it can keep operating if one is damaged or destroyed. Replacing the bespoke equipment could take years.
"You cannot down a Shahed drone, or a drone with optical cable attached. So we need reinforced-concrete sarcophagi around equipment", said Semeskevicius.
The equipment needs to be artificially cooled down inside the sarcophagi, which adds to the cost.
"Without all this, we might not have power at all", he said.
Lithuania's military is advising Litgrid on physically securing critical energy infrastructure and resistance to modern threats, officials told Reuters.
THE MOST COSTLY INTERCONNECTION
Later this month, Lithuania will ask the EU to cover at least half of the Gizai costs, Energy Minister Lukas Savickas told Reuters.
Litgrid says the secured substation will cost at least €48 million more than planned earlier. The price could increase further if "geopolitical circumstances" worsen.
"Our consistent position is... these costs should not fall solely on our shoulders," Savickas said.
A senior Polish official echoed that view, saying countries that border Russia risk losing competitiveness if their companies are stuck with the bill for additional security.
Harmony Link cannot become "the most costly interconnection in Europe", Wojciech Wrochna, Poland's deputy energy minister in charge of strategic energy infrastructure, said, calling for the EU to boost financing of the grid security measures.
"Our European partners need to change their mindset," Wrochna told Reuters. "The issue extends beyond Harmony Link. It affects the entire energy system."
Last year the Baltic states and Poland asked the EU for €382 million to help secure key parts of the existing grid but only €112 million was granted.
The European Commission did not reply to Reuters' request for comment. REUTERS

articles.title: EU removes two oligarchs from Russia sanctions list as deadline looms
articles.body:
The EU has agreed to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies accused of supporting the war on Ukraine for the next three years.
With an end-of-Tuesday deadline looming to preserve the Russia blacklist, the EU’s 27 member states found a compromise that meant delisting the two oligarchs in spite of very few countries wanting this outcome. EU sanctions have to be approved unanimously.
France stunned and infuriated EU governments this month when it called for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek national, to be removed from the list on “national security” grounds, reported to refer to a prisoner exchange deal involving French nationals and Azerbaijan.
Luxembourg then asked for the same treatment for Fridman, the Russian-Israeli magnate, who is suing the Grand Duchy for $16bn (£12bn) for freezing his assets.
The exemptions angered many EU countries which believe it sets a bad precedent by allowing member states to weaken sanctions in defence of national interests.
Ukraine criticised the removal of the men from the sanctions list as unacceptable. Shortly after the decision emerged, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on social media: “No name on the sanctions list is there by accident: each one represents a reason why this war started and continues to this day.”
The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called the decision “shameful and unjustifiable” on X. “Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he added.
In order to enable the delistings that many EU member states found unpalatable, it was proposed that the sanctions be rolled over for 36 months, rather than the usual six.
A spokesperson for Ireland’s EU presidency, which brokered the talks, said the bloc had reached “a difficult compromise”. They said: “Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”
A decision had been expected earlier this week, but Latvia’s government, facing parliamentary elections on 3 October, announced a last-minute objection to the delistings on Monday. Latvia’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, said late on Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise and instructed his foreign minister to enter talks with Paris and Brussels to find a solution.
Diplomats said Latvia had finally agreed to abstain on the two delistings. The blacklist includes Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, as well as Duma deputies, the country’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.
Senior EU officials have promised to present about 1,600 new designations – individuals and entities involved in the Russian military industrial complex – to foreign ministers next month. But the latest standoff, which followed the tortuous agreement on the EU’s 21st round of sanctions in July, suggests the process could be difficult.

articles.title: Trump announced a “massive” potash deal with Belarus—Lukashenka said the same day there is no spare potash to sell
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced a "massive deal" to buy Belarusian potash at prices far below what the US pays Canada, but Belarusian dictator Alyaksandr Lukashenka publicly contradicted him the same day, saying Belarus has no spare volumes to sell.
Washington has spent a year courting Lukashenka with sanctions relief and envoy visits in pursuit of both prisoner releases and trade openings—but the potash episode shows the limits of that courtship when the dictator's own supply chain cannot deliver what the US President has already promised his voters.
Trump promised cheaper potash for American farmers
Trump wrote on Truth Social on 21 September:
"The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus. The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers."
Potash is a key ingredient in fertilizer. Canada is the world's largest supplier—the US takes 53% of Canadian potash exports, and 80% of the potash American farms use comes from Canada. Canadian potash remains exempt from US tariffs despite the ongoing trade war between the two countries.
The announcement came as Trump's trade dispute with Ottawa deepened—he recently called Canada a "terrible trade partner," and on 16 September European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate EU membership, which Trump said could be a "hostile act."
Lukashenka said all output is contracted
The same day, Lukashenka told officials Belarus cannot deliver. "Even if we wanted to supply potash to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes—everything is contracted," he said during a meeting with the head of Belarus's State Customs Committee, Uladzimir Arlouski.
Arlouski reported that 85% of all Belarusian exports and imports now move eastward—primarily to China, other Asian countries, and Russia. Budget revenues grew almost 3.5% over eight months, and 5.2% so far this month.
A deal built on sanctions relief and prisoner swaps
The potash announcement followed a year-long US effort to engage Lukashenka. Washington lifted sanctions on Belarus's potash industry in exchange for the release of hundreds of political prisoners. US special envoy John Cole has played the central role, meeting Lukashenka last week and securing the release of 25 prisoners—far fewer than the 200 he had previously promised.
Over the course of Cole's effort, at least several hundred people have been freed, among them Nobel Peace Prize laureate Ales Bialiatski and Siarhei Tsikhanouski, husband of the internationally recognized winner of Belarus's 2020 presidential election. But human rights groups and freed prisoners say Lukashenka runs a "carousel"—arresting new political opponents to replace the ones he releases. Lukashenka denied this. "There are no political prisoners in Belarus," he claimed during last week's meeting with Cole.
With US midterms six weeks away on 3 November and the Republican Party struggling in the polls, Trump has been scrambling for wins on fuel and food prices. The same week, he urged Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian refineries, blaming Ukraine rather than his own war with Iran for record US diesel prices—a move a senior European official told Politico was a search for "scapegoats."

articles.title: Zelensky receives no clear answer from Trump to request to give air defense missiles
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky said he had not received a clear answer from US President Donald Trump to the request to help Ukraine with missiles for Patriot air defense systems.
"I did not receive a concrete response to the request to help with missiles for Patriots. We have a [shortage] of them," Zelensky said at a press conference.
According to Zelensky, he is ready to use various schemes to obtain missiles for air defense.
On September 8, EU countries approved an exception that allows Ukraine to purchase missiles for Patriot systems using funds from the EU’s 90 billion euro funding program. Kiev previously officially requested permission from the European Commission to purchase the US missiles, as the program operates under a rule that gives priority to the weapons purchases from European military companies.
The United Kingdom’s Defense Ministry said that the country will allocate 100 million pounds ($135 million) to purchase missiles for Patriot systems from the United States for Ukraine’s needs.
Moscow has repeatedly emphasized that the West’s supply of weapons to Kiev and assistance in training Ukrainian military personnel only prolong the conflict and do not change the situation on the battlefield.

articles.title: Trump’s U.N. Address Offers a Doctrine of Peace Through Force
articles.body:
In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, President Donald Trump spun a familiar web of rhetoric regarding U.S. foreign policy—one that highlights force as a method of achieving peace.
In a speech that moved from Iran to Venezuela, Cuba, and beyond, Trump presented something approaching a foreign-policy doctrine: American military might is not the alternative to diplomacy but the leverage that makes it possible.
David Satterfield, Director of Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy, tells TIME that the speech Tuesday demonstrates a position held by the Trump Administration that “force is the only currency of value.”
“The strong do as they will and the weak suffer as they must,” he says, further characterizing the approach.
In Trump’s telling, strength is not merely a deterrent. It is something to be used—through military action and economic isolation—to force negotiations or impose an outcome.
How Trump defines ‘peace through strength’
Trump has repeatedly distilled his foreign policy strategy into three words: “peace through strength.” The examples he gave of this policy in action illustrate how he may see the U.S. functioning as a global enforcer going forward.
His definition of the phrase has previously been suggested by its use in Department of Defense ads and in his online endorsements of fellow Republicans. He recently credited this approach for the joint U.S.-Israel strikes that initiated the current conflict with Iran, posting to Truth Social in March: “PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH TO PUT IT MILDLY!!!”
Trump’s approach also encompasses economic coercion. In the case of Iran, he said the U.S. had initially offered economic cooperation, turned to military action when Tehran refused, and was now seeking its “complete economic isolation” to push it back toward negotiations.
Trump grouped Cuba among those affected by U.S. economic pressure campaigns on Tuesday. He described a government under mounting strain and predicted political change, declaring that Cuba was a “failed” nation but that “freedom will be coming.” Cuban delegates departed in protest.
Yet Trump presented such coercion as compatible with his role as a global peacemaker. He claimed credit for resolving eight wars since returning to office, although that claim has been widely disputed.
In tandem, these elements suggest that Trump sees taking action as a superior means of enacting change. He proposes the approaches as being almost diametrically opposed: While others only speak of making a difference, he acts.
“While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them,” Trump said in front of the General Assembly. “While others have talked of courage, America has shown it.”
Satterfield says that this speech is mostly “old wine rebottled” for Trump. But it clarified how the President is applying his longstanding ideas today: using military action and economic coercion not merely to deter adversaries, but to force negotiations and shape political outcomes.
Trump defends military force against Iran and drug cartels
While Trump sees Iran as an example of his “peace through strength” ethos, the conflict is ongoing, and it remains to be seen how it fits into the pattern that he is hoping to establish.
Addressing the topic seemed all but unavoidable heading into the General Assembly. In doing so, Trump said that he had a choice ahead of him: Move forward with a peace deal or “annihilate the Islamic Republic.”
The comments came amid stalled negotiations in the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?” he asked. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Members of Iran’s delegation walked out during Trump’s remarks, an immediate demonstration of the gulf between his coercive message and the adversary that he may hope to persuade by it.
In his speech, he also issued threats against cartel leaders, defending his campaign of drone strikes against suspected drug boats in the Caribbean. These strikes have been criticized by international organizations, legal experts, and human rights groups, which state that the military actions violate international law and constitute extrajudicial killings.
“The cartels are the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere—not good people,” he said. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled, or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing.”
But while these messages are largely meant to promote the very strength that Trump relies upon in his endeavors, the potency of his remarks may be dwindling amid contested claims of success.
Venezuela is Trump’s ‘peace through strength’ model. But Iran is testing its limits
Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, a fellow for the Middle East at the Baker Institute, tells TIME that Trump’s speech seems “consistent with the narrative of American dominance” that he has long used to justify military action.
Trump suggested Tuesday that he considers Venezuela a leading example. In January, the U.S. military launched Operation Absolute Resolve—a nighttime raid in Caracas that captured Venezuela’s president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. Both were transported to New York City to face federal drug-trafficking indictments.
The move paved the way for a transition of power in Venezuela, with former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez ascending to the role of acting President. It also led to an August agreement giving a U.S.-linked venture a controlling stake and long-term development rights in fields containing an estimated 65 billion barrels of oil. Trump said the deal “more than doubles” American oil reserves.
“We’re working closely with the leaders of Venezuela to forge a much better future for the Venezuelan people,” Trump said in his speech. “Last month we signed the largest oil deal in history, covering 65 billion barrels of oil, which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously.”
Trump also suggested that U.S. actions had established peace and a route to prosperity for Venezuelans. However, with an acting President who is yet to be elected making deals that may take years to reach fruition, and are likely to draw legal challenges in the meantime, the full picture remains to be seen.
But there is one thing the Venezuela operation might have helped accomplish, which is to establish a potential pattern of a U.S. foreign policy that is defined by unilateral intervention. Following a large show of force, Trump has been quick to claim victory, even while the impact of U.S. involvement is still playing out for the people whom it directly affects.
Another example is the conflict between Israel and Hamas. In his remarks, Trump gave himself credit for ending the war in Gaza, even though key aspects of the peace deal Trump helped broker in October 2025—including Hamas’s disarmament, a long-term governance plan, and the delivery of needed humanitarian aid in Gaza—are largely stalled.
Perceived success in Venezuela “arguably triggered the overreach that we saw in the decision to begin military operations against Iran without a Plan B if initial objectives were not achieved,” Ulrichsen says.
But the limitations of such rhetoric are most “visible” in the Iran conflict, according to Ulrichsen, who says the U.S. has not been able to “translate rhetoric into gains on the ground.”
Trump has repeatedly predicted that the war would end after the November midterm elections, saying last week that it would end “immediately after” them. He endorsed this belief on Tuesday, as well. Trump initially told reporters that U.S. envoys had held a “very good” three-hour meeting with “mediators of Iran."
“They had a very good meeting, and we'll see how it turns out. But certainly, it's to their advantage to make a deal, and we can do that,” he said.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior nonresident fellow at the Center for International Policy, emphasized the point that concrete outcomes in the Middle East may prove critical for Trump.
“President Trump’s ‘peace through strength’ approach has yet to produce the agreement he wants with Iran,” Mortazavi says. “Trump’s argument leaves a central question unanswered: How does further destruction secure an agreement on Washington’s terms when the pressure so far has not?”
“For now, Trump can point to the damage U.S. forces have inflicted, but the war’s central political disputes remain unresolved,” she adds.
The outcomes of these most recent efforts—and whether they moved the needle on peace efforts—remain undetermined. Subsequently, Trump turned to the same takeaway that he shared in his speech, which is that Iran is facing either “potential greatness or obliteration.”
“It does seem as if such rhetoric is producing diminishing results as his tone gradually loses its shock value,” Ulrichsen observes.

articles.title: Russia Has Scaled Up Its Use of Guided Bombs to the Level of U.S. Air Campaigns
articles.body:
The Russian Air Force has increased the monthly intensity of its guided bomb strikes to the level seen in some U.S. air campaigns.
Militarnyi conducted this analysis based on reports from the U.S. Department of Defense and research by RUSI analysts.
In August 2026, the Russian military deployed 8,766 air bombs equipped with universal guidance and correction modules (UMPK) over Ukrainian territory.
The average was 283 munitions dropped per day.
This rate of high-precision weapon use exceeds that of the U.S. Air Force during Operation Epic Fury against Iran.
At that time, American pilots dropped approximately 211–237 guided bombs per day.
At the same time, the current intensity of strikes by the Russian Air Force remains nearly half that of the scale of American bombing during the main phase of the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when the number of precision-guided munitions used reached about 509 per day.
American JDAM kits and Russian UMPK modules are based on a common design concept.
Thanks to these systems, specialists are converting existing stocks of conventional free-fall bombs into high-precision weapons without the need to manufacture new munitions.
The United States has been building up its arsenal of such weapons since the late 1990s, while the Russian defense industry scaled up the mass production of UMPK in a short period of time, already during a full-scale war. Despite this, the comparison demonstrates the scale of Russia’s use of aerial weapons against Ukraine.
Militarnyi previously reported that during the last ten days of July, Russia attacked Pavlohrad—located approximately 75 kilometers from the front line—three times with guided aerial bombs. This may indicate a resumption of the use of UMPB-5R aerial bombs equipped with jet engines.
Read more in the article: “8,766 Air Bombs in a Month: How Russia Has Scaled Up Its Use of Air-Launched Bombs to the Level of U.S. Air Campaigns.”

articles.title: Latvia to impose national sanctions on Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman after EU compromise
articles.body:
Latvia to impose national sanctions on Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman after EU compromise
Latvia will impose national sanctions on the Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman after making concessions and lifting its veto on their removal from the EU sanctions list.
Source: European Pravda, citing a statement by the Latvian government on 22 September
Details: Latvia's Cabinet of Ministers has instructed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to immediately draw up a proposal, legal justification and the necessary draft legislation to enable Latvia to impose national sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman.
Quote: "Latvia will continue to use all legal instruments at its disposal to prevent the unfreezing of these individuals' funds and economic resources in Latvia."
More details: The Cabinet of Ministers also said that at a closed meeting on 22 September, it had agreed on Latvia's position on extending EU sanctions against Russia. The deal ensured that personal sanctions against more than 2,600 Russian supporters of the war and related individuals and entities would be extended for the next three years. Up until now, the decision has had to be taken every six months.
During the procedure for the adoption of the decision by the Council of the EU, however, Latvia's representative will abstain from voting in order to maintain and publicly express Latvia's political opposition to the lifting of EU sanctions on the two oligarchs.
"Throughout the negotiations with the leaders of EU member states, Latvia opposed the removal of politically motivated individuals from the individual sanctions list and was the only EU member state to maintain this position until the very end. It was the morally right position, and our allies in Ukraine appreciated it," Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said.
He added that "this was not a choice between a good and a bad decision, but between a bad one and a much worse one – a choice between changing the status of two individuals and the future of the entire sanctions regime".
Quote from Kulbergs: "By deciding to continue imposing sanctions on these individuals, we have achieved an outcome that is more beneficial for Latvia, Ukraine and Europe in the long term."
Background:
- Amid the announcement of Riga's decision, it was reported that French President Emmanuel Macron has agreed to begin talks with Latvia on joining France's nuclear deterrence initiative, and that France has committed to strengthening its military presence in Latvia.
- European Pravda sources in French diplomatic circles explained why Paris wanted to lift sanctions on Usmanov. It later emerged that France planned to "exchange" Usmanov's delisting for the release of several French citizens who are currently in prison in Azerbaijan.

articles.title: Netanyahu to cut short NYC trip amid protests, Mamdani threat
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Netanyahu to cut short NYC visit amid protests, Mamdani arrest threat
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dramatically shortened his visit to New York for the UN General Assembly, amid planned protests, heightened security and tensions with Mayor Zohran Mamdani over the International Criminal Court warrant for his arrest.
Netanyahu is expected to arrive in the US on Thursday morning, address the General Assembly at 2pm New York time and leave for Israel later that evening, according to Israeli media reports.
The Israeli leader is not expected to spend a single night in the US, cutting what had initially been planned as a longer visit to just several hours. He has also cancelled a planned stop in Texas to meet billionaire Elon Musk and will not take Israeli journalists aboard his official "Wing of Zion" aircraft.
Israeli media cited planned protests and security concerns among the reasons for the unusually brief visit.
According to Ynet, Netanyahu's plane is expected to avoid New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport and instead land in neighbouring New Jersey.
The outlet linked the arrangements partly to tensions with Mamdani, who has repeatedly called for Netanyahu to face arrest over the ICC warrant.
Other Israeli reporting, however, has attributed the decision to avoid JFK to logistical and security considerations surrounding Netanyahu's aircraft.
Mamdani has been an outspoken critic of Netanyahu and previously pledged to have the Israeli leader arrested if he travelled to New York, citing the ICC warrant issued against him in November 2024.
The mayor acknowledged in July, however, that New York City does not independently possess the legal authority to enforce the warrant.
"It is clear that we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant," Mamdani said at the time, while calling on the US federal government to join the ICC and execute it.
He has nevertheless maintained that Netanyahu is not welcome in New York and has continued to describe him as a war criminal over Israel's actions in Gaza.
The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli defence minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, saying there were reasonable grounds to believe they bore criminal responsibility for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Israel's war on Gaza.
Israel rejects the allegations and does not recognise the court's jurisdiction. The US is also not a member of the ICC.
US President Donald Trump said in July that Netanyahu would not be arrested in the United States.
Heavy security and protests expected
Netanyahu is expected to receive unusually heavy security protection during his brief stay, with US Secret Service involvement in preparations for the visit reportedly greater than usual.
Large demonstrations are also expected in New York during his visit.
Haaretz reported that Netanyahu is preparing for a hostile reception both on the streets and inside the General Assembly, where Israeli officials anticipate that ambassadors and other delegates could walk out or stage protests during his speech.
A mass walkout took place when Netanyahu addressed the General Assembly last year.
Mamdani has said he does not plan to participate in protests against Netanyahu during the visit and has been coordinating with the New York Police Department over security surrounding UNGA.
Netanyahu is not expected to meet Trump during the trip, and a meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also not been confirmed.
His address comes around a month before Israel's general election, with Israeli media reporting that the speech is expected to focus heavily on Iran while also being aimed at a domestic Israeli audience.
Israeli officials are meanwhile hoping protests inside the General Assembly will be smaller than last year, amid international attention on the war with Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Israel continues to occupy most of the Gaza Strip and carry out deadly air strikes, shelling and gunfire despite the October 2025 ceasefire.
More than 73,900 Palestinians have been killed and nearly 175,000 wounded since October 2023, including around 1,400 killed since the ceasefire took effect.
Most of Gaza's roughly 2.1 million people remain displaced, while Israeli restrictions continue to impede the entry of critical humanitarian and reconstruction supplies.

articles.title: Ukrainian SPYS Interceptor Drone Shoots Down Geran-5 Missile
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces shot down a Russian Geran-5 small cruise missile using a SPYS interceptor drone.
The GAU community published the video on its X account.
The footage shows the aircraft being shot down at a speed of about 200 km/h, likely due to a technical malfunction of the Russian missile’s jet engine.
In July, Ukrainian company WIY Drones presented the SPYS interceptor, which can engage targets traveling at speeds of up to 600 km/h.
Whilst Ukrainian manufacturers are urgently improving their means to counter the new, significantly upgraded Russian Geran-5s, there is now also good news from Germany. I received a video from a credible source showing the successful interception of a Geran-5 by the new SPYS… pic.twitter.com/IUj6xCcq5s
— GAU (@deaidua) September 21, 2026
A company representative told Militarnyi that the interceptor is primarily intended to engage jet-powered Geran drones.
To enable the UAV to reach such speeds, WIY Drones developed its own electronic components. This allows the drone to operate under extreme loads.
The SPYS interceptor uses Ukrainian-made motors from Motor-G, developed according to WIY Drones’ technical specifications.
The drone carries a 300-gram warhead, can engage targets up to 12 km away, and has a flight time of five minutes.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian oil refineries in Samara and Ufa
articles.body:
Ukraine hits Russian oil refineries in Samara and Ufa
Units from the Ukrainian defence forces struck two key oil refining facilities in Russia on the night of 21-22 September.
Sources: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine; Special Operations Forces (SOF)
Details: The Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara was struck.
The Special Operations Forces said the attack was carried out by Special Operations Forces' Deep Strike units jointly with the Unmanned Systems Forces and Defence Intelligence of Ukraine. Several drones reached their targets, causing a large-scale fire at the facility.
The Kuibyshev oil refinery is one of the largest oil refining facilities in Russia's Samara group and is part of the Rosneft structure. It has a refining capacity of around 7 million tonnes of oil per year. The refinery produces petrol, diesel fuel, fuel oil and more than 30 other petroleum products.
The Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim oil refinery in Ufa, Republic of Bashkortostan, Russia, was also struck, with a fire reported on the premises.
Bashneft-Ufaneftekhim has a refining capacity of around 7.5 million tonnes of oil per year. The facility carries out deep oil refining and produces petrol, diesel and boiler fuel, liquefied gases, sulphur and other petroleum products.
Products from both refineries are used to meet the needs of the Russian military.

articles.title: New group of US troops 'on its way' to Lithuania, says the Lithuanian president
articles.body:
Trump deploys fresh US troops to Lithuania, says country’s president, amid cuts in Europe
- A new rotation of US troops is already on its way to Lithuania, according to President Gitanas Nauseda.
- Nauseda thanked President Donald Trump and the US administration, calling the presence vital for Lithuania and regional security.
- Despite US troop withdrawals from Europe, Lithuania emphasises the US military presence as key for deterrence and collective defence.
AI generated
VILNIUS - The United States has confirmed that it is sending a new rotation of troops to Lithuania, the Baltic NATO country said on Sept 22, ending a period of uncertainty over whether the US military would replace forces that returned home this summer.
The US is withdrawing thousands of troops from bases in Europe, and Lithuania, which shares borders with Russia and Belarus, said in June it had learned that the US was reviewing its future military presence in the country.
“I have just received confirmation that the new rotation of US troops is already on its way to Lithuania,” President Gitanas Nauseda wrote in a post on social media X.
Nauseda thanked President Donald Trump and the US administration, adding that this was important for Lithuania and for the security of the region.
“The US military presence in Lithuania is an indispensable part of our deterrence and collective defence,” Nauseda said.
He did not say how many service members the next rotation would contain.
Since 2019, the US has usually deployed an armoured battalion of about 1,000 troops in the country.
Lithuania‘s Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said the US deployment was “returning to large numbers”, but did not provide details.
“Lithuania is indeed a strong and reliable partner, and today we received proof of that,” Budrys said in a statement.
The US embassy in Vilnius did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside of regular business hours. REUTERS

articles.title: Ukraine’s Donetsk counteroffensive wins not by force but by stealth: it gathers troops under Russian nose and seizes two villages before they react
articles.body:
Ukrainian troops gathered for an assault on two Russian-held villages, and the Russians never saw them coming. A captain of the 60th Mechanized Brigade, with the callsign Akhmet, says the concealed buildup near Derylove and Drobysheve was what allowed his units to take the villages once Operation Vivaldi began, Suspilne reports.
The account fills in how Vivaldi actually takes ground: not by overwhelming force but by concealment, timing, and technology. Only the first phase of the "Operation Vivaldi" counteroffensive, which the Third Army Corps is running near Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast, has cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltrators and liberated another 10 square kilometers of territory.
Concealment set up the assault
The brigade's task was to free Derylove and take control of Drobysheve. The key, Akhmet says, was accumulating forces as covertly as possible in Drobysheve and on the outskirts of Derylove, so the units could begin exactly on schedule.
The Russians, he believes, failed to spot the buildup because Ukraine had done its reconnaissance well during the planning and preparation. Constant coordination with neighboring units, sharing information, and lending help mattered too. The point was to keep the movement and massing hidden until the appointed hour, so nothing tipped the Russians off before the assault opened.
The captain coordinates the fight
As a battle captain, Akhmet oversaw the tasks set by brigade command and the work of several strands at once: reconnaissance, drones, electronic warfare, and air defense.
"We determine where the enemy sits, we inflict fire damage on Russian soldiers, and we cover our groups on the ground," he said.
The job was to find the Russians, strike them, and shield the assault teams as they moved up.
Timing cleared the infantry's path
The brigade also located where Russian drones were taking off and hit those launch points at set times, to keep enemy operators from scouting and firing on the Ukrainian troops working below. Getting the timing right was the whole point, Akhmet explains, so the infantry could move to its positions and reach cover without being caught in the open.
The two villages were a piece of a larger aim: the Institute for the Study of War has assessed that Vivaldi disrupted Russia's plan to encircle the fortified belt of Donetsk cities.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine, Russia 'going to make a deal,' discusses Patriot missile production
articles.body:
Merve Aydogan
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
US President Donald Trump said he believes a deal between Ukraine and Russia is imminent as he held a meeting Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly's high-level week in New York.
"We have a very good relationship going, the two of us. The president (Zelenskyy) and I are trying to figure out the solution, and I think it's going to happen. I really do," said Trump. "But the relationship is very strong, and with Europe it's very strong. And you saw what just happened with Greenland, which was something very special.”
Asked whether he still believed Ukraine could reclaim all its territory, Trump said, "Well, I think they're going to make a deal, and I don't want to say what the deal is. We talk about it a lot, including with President (Vladimir) Putin, and I think something's going to happen."
"But, certainly they are very good fighters. Really, they could be proud of themselves," he said, calling Ukraine's leadership "very capable."
Pointing to Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refining capacity, Trump said, "The strikes inside Russia on the refining capacity and the diesel, it seems like that's been a serious hit on the Russians. It's also a serious hit on the price of diesel."
"I think they (Putin and Zelenskyy) both want to see the war end. To be honest with you, it's time. A lot of people being killed, and they don't want that," said Trump.
On possible Patriot missile production in Ukraine, Trump said, "We're talking about that. We'll be talking about that now,” he said. “Very capable production. I mean, we talk about it all the time. Very capable people. Really amazingly capable people."
Zelenskyy said he hoped "we will end this war, and President Trump will help us to end this war," adding it was needed "as quick as possible before winter."

articles.title: Germany cut Russian gas after 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Now, its far-right AfD party is in talks with Gazprom to bring it back, and Kremlin welcomes decision
articles.body:
Germany's far-right AfD has confirmed it is in talks with Gazprom to bring Russian gas back to Germany. Its foreign-policy speaker met the Russian gas giant's chief in Moscow to discuss resuming supplies, a step that would reverse the break with Russian energy Germany made after the 2022 invasion, the party told DW.
The AfD is openly working to undo one of the West's central responses to the war. Before 2022, Russia supplied about 55 percent of Germany's gas, a dependence federal officials later blamed for Berlin's slow initial reaction to the invasion.
Cutting it cost Moscow its biggest European market. Restoring it would hand back one of its largest revenue streams at a time when energy sales fund the war.
The Kremlin has already publicly welcomed the AfD’s efforts to engage in dialogue with Moscow. Dmitriy Peskov, press secretary for Russian President Vladimir Putin, has also reacted positively to the party’s growing popularity.
The AfD confirms the Moscow talks
The confirmation came from Beatrix von Storch, deputy leader of the AfD's Bundestag faction.
The party's foreign-policy speaker, Markus Frohnmaier, was in Moscow and personally spoke with Mr. Miller of Gazprom, she said, referring to Alexei Miller, the company's chairman.
"Of course, we are interested in resuming trade. We need affordable energy and the widest possible supply, so we consider it in our interest to get supplies from Russia too, which is why we are holding these talks," she said.
The politics run through the east
The talks land as the AfD surges at the polls, topping recent votes in eastern Germany and in Berlin, contests in which Russia's war against Ukraine figured in the party's platform. Asked what signal those results send Moscow, von Storch cast the war less as foreign policy than as a domestic worry.
"Of course, it is an important topic. People fear war and that Germany will be drawn into it, let itself be drawn in, or directly enter it," she said.
